Such a conquest shall be obtained over it that it shall for ever disappear in those regions to which our Lord will bear his risen saints. And therefore will the saints hereupon sing their <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epinikion,</hi></hi> their <hi type="italic">song of triumph.</hi> Then, when this mortal shall have put on immortality, will death be swallowed up, for ever swallowed up, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis nikos.</hi></hi> Christ hinders it from swallowing his saints when they die; but, when they rise again, death shall, as to them, be swallowed for ever. And upon this destruction of death will they break out into a song of triumph. <div eID="gen31379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31380" type="x-p"/> 1. They will glory over death as a vanquished enemy, and insult this great and terrible destroyer: "<hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting?</hi> Where is now thy sting, thy power to hurt? What mischief hast thou done us? We are dead; but behold we live again, and shall die no more. Thou art vanquished and disarmed, and we are out of the reach of thy deadly dart. Where now is thy fatal artillery? Where are thy stores of death? We fear no further mischiefs from thee, nor heed thy weapons, but defy thy power, and despise thy wrath. And, <hi type="italic">O grave! where is thy victory?</hi> Where now is thy victory? What has become of it? Where are the spoils and trophies of it? Once we were thy prisoners, but the prison-doors are burst open, the locks and bolts have been forced to give way, our shackles are knocked off, and we are for ever released. Captivity is taken captive. The imaginary victor is conquered, and forced to resign his conquest and release his captives. Thy triumphs, grave, are at an end. The bonds of death are loosed, and we are at liberty, and are never more to be hurt by death, nor imprisoned in the grave." In a moment, the power of death, and the conquests and spoils of the grave, are gone; and, as to the saints, the very signs of them will not remain. Where are they? Thus will they raise themselves, when they become immortal, to the honour of their Saviour and the praise of divine grace: they shall glory over vanquished death. <div eID="gen31380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31381" type="x-p"/> 2. The foundation for this triumph is here intimated, (1.) In the account given whence death had its power to hurt: <hi type="italic">The sting of death is sin.</hi> This gives venom to his dart: this alone puts it into the power of death to hurt and kill. Sin unpardoned, and nothing else, can keep any under his power. And the <hi type="italic">strength of sin is the law;</hi> it is the divine threatening against the transgressors of the law, the curse there denounced, that gives power to sin. Note, Sin is the parent of death, and gives it all its hurtful power. <hi type="italic">By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Rom. v. 12</reference>. It is its cursed progeny and offspring. (2.) In the account given of the victory saints obtain over it through Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.56">v. 56</reference>. <hi type="italic">The sting of death is sin;</hi> but Christ, by dying, has taken out this sting. He has made atonement for sin; he has obtained remission of it. It may hiss therefore, but it cannot hurt. <hi type="italic">The strength of sin is the law;</hi> but the curse of the law is removed by our Redeemer's <hi type="italic">becoming a curse for us.</hi> So that sin is deprived of its strength and sting, through Christ, that is, by his incarnation, suffering, and death. Death may seize a believer, but cannot sting him, cannot hold him in his power. There is a day coming when the grave shall open, the bands of death be loosed, the dead saints revive, and become incorruptible and immortal, and put out of the reach of death for ever. And then will it plainly appear that, as to them, death will have lost its strength and sting; and all by the mediation of Christ, by his dying in their room. By dying, he conquered death, and spoiled the grave; and, through faith in him, believers become sharers in his conquests. They often rejoice beforehand, in the hope of this victory; and, when they arise glorious from the grave, they will boldly triumph over death. Note, It is altogether owing to the grace of God in Christ that sin is pardoned and death disarmed. The law puts arms into the hand of death, to destroy the sinner; but pardon of sin takes away this power from the law, and deprives death of its strength and sting. It is <hi type="italic">by the grace of God, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, that we are freely justified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Rom. iii. 24</reference>. It is no wonder, therefore, (3.) If this triumph of the saints over death should issue in thanksgiving to God: <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory through Christ Jesus, our Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.57">v. 57</reference>. The way to sanctify all our joy is to make it tributary to the praise of God. Then only do we enjoy our blessings and honours in a holy manner when God has his revenue of glory out of it, and we are free to pay it to him. And this really improves and exalts our satisfaction. We are conscious at once of having done our duty and enjoyed our pleasure. And what can be more joyous in itself than the saints' triumph over death, when they shall rise again? And shall they not then rejoice in the Lord, and be glad in the God of their salvation? Shall not their souls magnify the Lord? When he shows <hi type="italic">such wonders to the dead, shall they not arise and praise him?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.88.10">Ps. lxxxviii. 10</reference>. Those who remain under the power of death can have no heart to praise; but such conquests and triumphs will certainly tune the tongues of the saints to thankfulness and praise—praise for the victory (it is great and glorious in itself), and for the means whereby it is obtained (it is given of God through Christ Jesus), a victory obtained not by our power, but the power of God; not given because we are worthy, but because Christ is so, and has by dying obtained this conquest for us. Must not this circumstance endear the victory to us, and heighten our praise to God? Note, How many springs of joy to the saints and thanksgiving to God are opened by the death and resurrection, the sufferings and conquests, of our Redeemer! With what acclamations will saints rising from the dead applaud him! How will the heaven of heavens resound his praises for ever! <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God</hi> will be the burden of their song; and angels will join the chorus, and declare their consent with a loud Amen, Hallelujah.
entries.ff8e68817628221fdc2b4cf2dcf0dc304a0be463: <div eID="gen31381" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Obligations of Christians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31382" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">58</hi> Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. <div eID="gen31382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31383" type="x-p"/> In this verse we have the improvement of the whole argument, in an exhortation, enforced by a motive resulting plainly from it. <div eID="gen31383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31384" type="x-p"/> I. An exhortation, and this threefold:—1. That they should be stedfast—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hedraioi,</hi></hi> firm, fixed in the faith of the gospel, that gospel which he had preached and they had received, namely, <hi type="italic">That Christ died for our sins, and arose again the third day, according to the scriptures</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3-1Cor.15.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), and fixed in the faith of the glorious resurrection of the dead, which, as he had shown, had so near and necessary a connection with the former. "Do not let your belief of these truths be shaken or staggered. They are most certain, and of the last importance." Note, Christians should be stedfast believers of this great article of the resurrection of the dead. It is evidently founded on the death of Christ. <hi type="italic">Because he lives, his servants shall live also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.19">John xiv. 19</reference>. And it is of the last importance; a disbelief of a future life will open a way to all manner of licentiousness, and corrupt men's morals to the last degree. It will be easy and natural to infer hence that we may live like beasts, and eat and drink, for to-morrow we die. 2. He exhorts them to be <hi type="italic">immovable,</hi> namely, in their expectation of this great privilege of being raised incorruptible and immortal. Christians should not be moved away from this hope of this gospel (<reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col. i. 23</reference>), this glorious and blessed hope; they should not renounce nor resign their comfortable expectations. They are not vain, but solid hopes, built upon sure foundations, the purchase and power of their risen Saviour, and the promise of God, to whom it is impossible to lie—hopes that shall be their most powerful supports under all the pressures of life, the most effectual antidotes against the fears of death, and the most quickening motives to diligence and perseverance in Christian duty. Should they part with these hopes? Should they suffer them to be shaken? Note, Christians should live in the most firm expectation of a blessed resurrection. This hope should be an anchor to their souls, firm and sure, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.19">Heb. vi. 19</reference>. 3. He exhorts them <hi type="italic">to abound in the work of the Lord,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">always,</hi> in the Lord's service, in obeying the Lord's commands. They should be diligent and persevering herein, and going on towards perfection; they should be continually making advances in true piety, and ready and apt for every good work. The most cheerful duty, the greatest diligence, the most constant perseverance, become those who have such glorious hopes. Can we too much abound in zeal and diligence in the Lord's work, when we are assured of such abundant recompences in a future life? What vigour and resolution, what constancy and patience, should those hopes inspire! Note, Christians should not stint themselves as to their growth in holiness, but be always improving in sound religion, and abounding in the work of the Lord. <div eID="gen31384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31385" type="x-p"/> II. The motive resulting from the former discourse is that their <hi type="italic">labour shall not be in vain in the Lord;</hi> nay, they know it shall not. They have the best grounds in the world to build upon: they have all the assurance that can rationally be expected: as surely as Christ is risen, they shall rise; and Christ is as surely risen as the scriptures are true, and the word of God. The apostles saw him after his death, testified this truth to the world in the face of a thousand deaths and dangers, and confirmed it by miraculous powers received from him. Is there any room to doubt a fact so well attested? Note, True Christians have undoubted evidence that their labour will not be in vain in the Lord; not their most diligent services, nor their most painful sufferings; they will not be in vain, not be vain and unprofitable. Note, The labour of Christians will not be lost labour; they may lose for God, but they will lose nothing by him; nay, there is more implied than is expressed in this phrase: it means that they shall be abundantly rewarded. He will never be found unjust to forget their labour of love, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">Heb. vi. 10</reference>. Nay, he will do exceedingly abundantly above what they can now ask or think. Neither the services they do for him, nor the sufferings they endure for him here, are worthy to be compared with the joy hereafter to be revealed in them, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.18">Rom. viii. 18</reference>. Note, Those who serve God have good wages; they cannot do too much nor suffer too much for so good a Master. If they serve him now, they shall see him hereafter; if they suffer for him on earth, they shall reign with him in heaven; if they die for his sake, they shall rise again from the dead, be crowned with glory, honour, and immortality, and inherit eternal life.  <chapter eID="1Cor.15"/> <div eID="gen31385" type="x-p"/>

entries.eadbcf78aec6ca7c230b5b75a9e90b4dd2d7d5b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17088"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <div sID="gen33842" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.1-1Cor.15.58">1Co 15:1-58</reference>. The Resurrection Proved against the Deniers of It at Corinth.<div eID="gen33842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33843" type="x-p"/> Christ's resurrection rests on the evidence of many eye-witnesses, including Paul himself, and is the great fact preached as the groundwork of the Gospel: they who deny the resurrection in general, must deny that of Christ, and the consequence of the latter will be, that Christian preaching and faith are vain.<div eID="gen33843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17088"/><hi type="bold">1. Moreover--</hi>"Now" [Alford and Ellicott].<div eID="gen33844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I declare--</hi>literally, "I make known": it implies some degree of reproach that it should be now necessary to make it known to them afresh, owing to some of them "not having the knowledge of God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.34">1Co 15:34</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.11">Ga 1:11</reference>.<div eID="gen33845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein ye stand--</hi>wherein ye now take your stand. This is your present actual privilege, if ye suffer not yourselves to fall from your high standing. <div eID="gen33846" type="x-p"/>
entries.07936791269f6e3323f83ea56e2c1af65713bfb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17089"/><div sID="gen33847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17089"/><hi type="bold">2. ye are saved--</hi>rather, "ye are being saved."<div eID="gen33847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you--</hi>Able critics, Bengel and others, prefer connecting the words thus, "I declare unto you the Gospel (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.1">1Co 15:1</reference>) in what words I preached it unto you." Paul reminds them, or rather makes known to them, as if anew, not only the fact of the Gospel, but also with what words, and by what arguments, he preached it to them. Translate in that case, "if ye hold it fast." I prefer arranging as English Version, "By which ye are saved, if ye hold fast (in memory and personal appropriation) with what speech I preached it unto you."<div eID="gen33848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unless--</hi>which is impossible, your faith is vain, in resting on Christ's resurrection as an objective reality. <div eID="gen33849" type="x-p"/>
entries.39b86a86f148016fa615bd43163f446db876380e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17090"/><div sID="gen33850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17090"/><hi type="bold">3. I delivered unto you--</hi>A short creed, or summary of articles of faith, was probably even then existing; and a profession in accordance with it was required of candidates for baptism (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.37">Ac 8:37</reference>).<div eID="gen33850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first of all--</hi>literally, "among the foremost points" (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.2">He 6:2</reference>). The atonement is, in Paul's view, of primary importance.<div eID="gen33851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which I ... received--</hi>from Christ Himself by special revelation (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>).<div eID="gen33852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">died for our sins--</hi>that is, to atone FOR them; for taking away our sins (<reference osisRef="1John.3.5">1Jo 3:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>): "gave Himself for our sins" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">Is 53:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">2Co 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>). The "for" here does not, as in some passages, imply vicarious substitution, but "in behalf of" (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.3">He 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>). It does not, however, mean merely "on account of," which is expressed by a different Greek word (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>), (though in English Version translated similarly, "for").<div eID="gen33853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the scriptures--</hi>which "cannot be broken." Paul puts the testimony of Scripture above that of those who saw the Lord after His resurrection [Bengel]. So our Lord quotes <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>, in <reference osisRef="Luke.22.37">Lu 22:37</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">Psa 22:15</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>. <div eID="gen33854" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5da82840bfe2d27cedcb42e5537815a8937ebc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17091"/><div sID="gen33855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17091"/><hi type="bold">4. buried ... rose again--</hi>His burial is more closely connected with His resurrection than His death. At the moment of His death, the power of His inextinguishable life exerted itself (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.52">Mt 27:52</reference>). The grave was to Him not the destined receptacle of corruption, but an apartment fitted for entering into life (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.26-Acts.2.28">Ac 2:26-28</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen33855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rose again--</hi>Greek, "hath risen": the state thus begun, and its consequences, still continue. <div eID="gen33856" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f9d0467f9d15bfaeb95005df0f6225f516b7805: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17092"/><div sID="gen33857" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17092"/><hi type="bold">5. seen of Cephas--</hi>Peter (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.34">Lu 24:34</reference>).<div eID="gen33857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the twelve--</hi>The round number for "the Eleven" (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.33">Lu 24:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.36">36</reference>). "The Twelve" was their ordinary appellation, even when their number was not full. However, very possibly Matthias was present (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.22">Ac 1:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">23</reference>). Some of the oldest manuscripts and versions read, "the Eleven": but the best on the whole, "the Twelve." <div eID="gen33858" type="x-p"/>
entries.40a83e4d6efc02a438230a53108b850a22e07bc7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17093"/><div sID="gen33859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17093"/><hi type="bold">6. five hundred--</hi>This appearance was probably on the mountain (Tabor, according to tradition), in Galilee, when His most solemn and public appearance, according to His special promise, was vouchsafed (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.32">Mt 26:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.7">28:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">10, 16</reference>). He "appointed" this place, as one remote from Jerusalem, so that believers might assemble there more freely and securely. Alford's theory of Jerusalem being the scene, is improbable; as such a multitude of believers could not, with any safety, have met in one place in the metropolis, after His crucifixion there. The number of disciples (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.15">Ac 1:15</reference>) at Jerusalem shortly after, was one hundred and twenty, those in Galilee and elsewhere not being reckoned. Andronicus and Junius were, perhaps, of the number (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>): they are said to be "among the apostles" (who all were witnesses of the resurrection, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.22">Ac 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen33859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remain unto this present--</hi>and, therefore, may be sifted thoroughly to ascertain the trustworthiness of their testimony.<div eID="gen33860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fallen asleep--</hi>in the sure hope of awaking at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.60">Ac 7:60</reference>). <div eID="gen33861" type="x-p"/>
entries.3100995f19aee9c0b940b3a6644f5507ba078eb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17094"/><div sID="gen33862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17094"/><hi type="bold">7. seen of James--</hi>the Less, the brother of our Lord (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.19">Ga 1:19</reference>). The Gospel according to the Hebrews, quoted by Jerome [On Illustrious Men, p. 170 D.], records that "James swore he would not eat bread from the hour that he drank the cup of the Lord, till he should see Him rising again from the dead."<div eID="gen33862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the apostles--</hi>The term here includes many others besides "the Twelve" already enumerated (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.5">1Co 15:5</reference>): perhaps the seventy disciples (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.1">Lu 10:1</reference>) [Chrysostom]. <div eID="gen33863" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca9f098d3e5c150eb3da1392658d1e25ea608f89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17095"/><div sID="gen33864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17095"/><hi type="bold">8. One born out of due time--</hi>Greek, "the one abortively born": the abortion in the family of the apostles. As a child born before the due time is puny, and though born alive, yet not of the proper size, and scarcely worthy of the name of man, so "I am the least of the apostles," scarcely "meet to be called an apostle"; a supernumerary taken into the college of apostles out of regular course, not led to Christ by long instruction, like a natural birth, but by a sudden power, as those prematurely born [Grotius]. Compare the similar image from childbirth, and by the same spiritual power, the resurrection of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pe 1:3</reference>). "Begotten again by the resurrection of Jesus." Jesus' appearance to Paul, on the way to Damascus, is the one here referred to. <div eID="gen33864" type="x-p"/>
entries.a94186c15f2d0456419736936c781ae3d747b2dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17096"/><div sID="gen33865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17096"/><hi type="bold">9. least--</hi>The name, "Paulus," in Latin, means "least."<div eID="gen33865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I persecuted the church--</hi>Though God has forgiven him, Paul can hardly forgive himself at the remembrance of his past sin. <div eID="gen33866" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a4db641d3700e41329b5c9273c61dd3dbd922fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17097"/><div sID="gen33867" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17097"/><hi type="bold">10. by ... grace ... and his grace--</hi>The repetition implies the prominence which God's grace had in his mind, as the sole cause of his marvellous conversion and subsequent labors. Though "not meet to be called an apostle," grace has given him, in Christ, the meetness needed for the office. Translate as the Greek, "His grace which was (showed) towards me."<div eID="gen33867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what I am--</hi>occupying the honorable office of an apostle. Contrast with this the self-sufficient prayer of another Pharisee (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Lu 18:11</reference>).<div eID="gen33868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but I laboured--</hi>by God's grace (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.16">Php 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen33869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than they all--</hi>than any of the apostles (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.7">1Co 15:7</reference>).<div eID="gen33870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace of God ... with me--</hi>Compare "the Lord working with them" (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.20">Mr 16:20</reference>). The oldest manuscripts omit "which was." The "not I, but grace," implies, that though the human will concurred with God when brought by His Spirit into conformity with His will, yet "grace" so preponderated in the work, that his own co-operation is regarded as nothing, and grace as virtually the sole agent. (Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1Co 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">Mt 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2Co 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Php 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen33871" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9fb1eeb0c79b34744eb65b012e528caeda5fff8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17098"/><div sID="gen33872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17098"/><hi type="bold">11. whether it were I or they--</hi>(the apostles) who "labored more abundantly" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.10">1Co 15:10</reference>) in preaching, such was the substance of our preaching, namely, the truths stated in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">1Co 15:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.4">4</reference>. <div eID="gen33872" type="x-p"/>
entries.907dead68e53eb3232d5a56ff2f249be2095138d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17099"/><div sID="gen33873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17099"/><hi type="bold">12. if--</hi>Seeing that it is an admitted fact that Christ is announced by us eye-witnesses as having risen from the dead, how is it that some of you deny that which is a necessary consequence of Christ's resurrection, namely, the general resurrection?<div eID="gen33873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">some--</hi>Gentile reasoners (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.32">Ac 17:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.8">26:8</reference>) who would not believe it because they did not see "how" it could be (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.35">1Co 15:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.36">36</reference>). <div eID="gen33874" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ceced7ec4f0ac4b9f38380947a1e0b3d972fda6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17100"/><div sID="gen33875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17100"/>13. If there be no general resurrection, which is the consequent, then there can have been no resurrection of Christ, which is the antecedent. The head and the members of the body stand on the same footing: what does not hold good of them, does not hold good of Him either: His resurrection and theirs are inseparably joined (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20-1Cor.15.22">1Co 15:20-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.19">Joh 14:19</reference>). <div eID="gen33875" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b035836176d322ceb59a689ee29fb8bff74849b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17101"/><div sID="gen33876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17101"/><hi type="bold">14. your faith ... vain--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.11">1Co 15:11</reference>). The Greek for "vain" here is, empty, unreal: in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.17">1Co 15:17</reference>, on the other hand, it is, without use, frustrated. The principal argument of the first preachers in support of Christianity was that God had raised Christ from the dead (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.22">Ac 1:22</reference>; 2:32; 4:10, 33; 13:37; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>). If this fact were false, the faith built on it must be false too. <div eID="gen33876" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b7739ed3ee5d1cba7749c21779820af18c12a38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17102"/><div sID="gen33877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17102"/><hi type="bold">15. testified of God--</hi>that is, concerning God. The rendering of others is, "against God" [Vulgate, Estius, Grotius]: the Greek preposition with the genitive implies, not direct antagonism (as the accusative would mean), but indirect to the dishonor of God. English Version is probably better.<div eID="gen33877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if so be--</hi>as they assert. It is not right to tell untrue stories, though they are told and seem for the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Job.13.7">Job 13:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33878" type="x-p"/>
entries.4246d9055c410c4e01b650574682707a886bd1d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17103"/><div sID="gen33879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17103"/>16. The repetition implies the unanswerable force of the argument. <div eID="gen33879" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ecd1ec8f855e9e15714249ddc8e543b975626f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17104"/><div sID="gen33880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17104"/><hi type="bold">17. vain--</hi>Ye are, by the very fact (supposing the case to be as the skeptics maintained), frustrated of all which "your faith" appropriates: Ye are still under the everlasting condemnation of your sins (even in the disembodied state which is here referred to), from which Christ's resurrection is our justification (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>): "saved by his life" (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">Ro 5:10</reference>). <div eID="gen33880" type="x-p"/>
entries.c05bb1c0131ba0e9c4b4ec3fc86df7b03c4a14bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17105"/><div sID="gen33881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17105"/><hi type="bold">18. fallen asleep in Christ--</hi>in communion with Christ as His members. "In Christ's case the term used is death, to assure us of the reality of His suffering; in our case, sleep, to give us consolation: In His case, His resurrection having actually taken place, Paul shrinks not from the term death; in ours, the resurrection being still only a matter of hope, he uses the term falling asleep" [Photius, Quæstiones Amphilochiæ, 197].<div eID="gen33881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perished--</hi>Their souls are lost; they are in misery in the unseen world. <div eID="gen33882" type="x-p"/>
entries.c49141d7f8ed5558ab499e7d8ce52285cd0b2582: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17106"/><div sID="gen33883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17106"/>19. If our hopes in Christ were limited to this life only, we should be, of all men, most to be pitied; namely, because, while others live unmolested, we are exposed to every trial and persecution, and, after all, are doomed to bitter disappointment in our most cherished hope; for all our hope of salvation, even of the soul (not merely of the body), hangs on the resurrection of Christ, without which His death would be of no avail to us (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pe 1:3</reference>). The heathen are "without hope" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>). We should be even worse, for we should be also without present enjoyment (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>). <div eID="gen33883" type="x-p"/>
entries.f404fa1974d723dafc1ffe7a692baf3e976080c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17107"/><div sID="gen33884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17107"/><hi type="bold">20. now--</hi>as the case really is.<div eID="gen33884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and become--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen33885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first-fruits--</hi>the earnest or pledge, that the whole resurrection harvest will follow, so that our faith is not vain, nor our hope limited to this life. The time of writing this Epistle was probably about the Passover (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1Co 5:7</reference>); the day after the Passover sabbath was that for offering the first-fruits (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.10">Le 23:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.11">11</reference>), and the same was the day of Christ's resurrection: whence appears the appropriateness of the image. <div eID="gen33886" type="x-p"/>
entries.36301e785ccf255f533ef2e072abc713293b06d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17108"/><div sID="gen33887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17108"/><hi type="bold">21. by man ... by man--</hi>The first-fruits are of the same nature as the rest of the harvest; so Christ, the bringer of life, is of the same nature as the race of men to whom He brings it; just as Adam, the bringer of death, was of the same nature as the men on whom he brought it. <div eID="gen33887" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b829a3c9909c6e55c837f4019ecd942ad16808f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17109"/><div sID="gen33888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17109"/><hi type="bold">22. in Adam all--</hi>in union of nature with Adam, as representative head of mankind in their fall.<div eID="gen33888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ ... all--</hi>in union of nature with Christ, the representative head of mankind in their recovery. The life brought in by Christ is co-extensive with the death brought in by Adam. <div eID="gen33889" type="x-p"/>
entries.a25f53b7de76367de5b6a3fca8df5772925da722: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17110"/><div sID="gen33890" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17110"/><hi type="bold">23. But every man in his own order--</hi>rather, "rank": the Greek is not in the abstract, but concrete: image from troops, "each in his own regiment." Though all shall rise again, let not any think all shall be saved; nay, each shall have his proper place, Christ first (<reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col 1:18</reference>), and after Him the godly who die in Christ (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>), in a separate band from the ungodly, and then "the end," that is, the resurrection of the rest of the dead. Christian churches, ministers, and individuals seem about to be judged first "at His coming" (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.1-Matt.25.30">Mt 25:1-30</reference>); then "all the nations" (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46">Mt 25:31-46</reference>). Christ's own flock shall share His glory "at His coming," which is not to be confounded with "the end," or general judgment (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.4-Rev.6.11">Re 20:4-6, 11</reference>-<reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">15</reference>). The latter is not in this chapter specially discussed, but only the first resurrection, namely, that of the saints: not even the judgment of Christian hollow professors (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.1-Matt.25.30">Mt 25:1-30</reference>) at His coming, is handled, but only the glory of them "that are Christ's," who alone in the highest sense "obtain the resurrection from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.14">Lu 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.35">20:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.11">Php 3:11</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Phil.3.11">Php 3:11</reference>). The second coming of Christ is not a mere point of time, but a period beginning with the resurrection of the just at His appearing, and ending with the general judgment. The ground of the universal resurrection is the union of all mankind in nature with Christ, their representative Head, who has done away with death, by His own death in their stead: the ground of the resurrection of believers is not merely this, but their personal union with Him as their "Life" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>), effected causatively by the Holy Spirit, and instrumentally by faith as the subjective, and by ordinances as the objective means. <div eID="gen33890" type="x-p"/>
entries.97b35870a0f4fc877e588996f10a0c8882f2da22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17111"/><div sID="gen33891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17111"/><hi type="bold">24. Then--</hi>after that: next in the succession of "orders" or "ranks."<div eID="gen33891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the end--</hi>the general resurrection, and final judgment and consummation (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.46">Mt 25:46</reference>).<div eID="gen33892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered up ... kingdom to ... Father--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="John.13.3">Joh 13:3</reference>). Seeming at variance with <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Da 7:14</reference>, "His dominion is an everlasting dominion which shall not pass away." Really, His giving up of the mediatorial kingdom to the Father, when the end for which the mediatorial economy was established has been accomplished, is altogether in harmony with its continuing everlastingly. The change which shall then take place, shall be in the manner of administration, not in the kingdom itself; God shall then come into direct connection with the earth, instead of mediatorially, when Christ shall have fully and finally removed everything that severs asunder the holy God and a sinful earth (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). The glory of God is the final end of Christ's mediatorial office (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>). His co-equality with the Father is independent of the latter, and prior to it, and shall, therefore, continue when its function shall have ceased. His manhood, too, shall everlastingly continue, though, as now, subordinate to the Father. The throne of the Lamb (but no longer mediatorial) as well as of God, shall be in the heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>). The unity of the Godhead, and the unity of the Church, shall be simultaneously manifested at Christ's second coming. Compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.21-John.17.24">Joh 17:21-24</reference>. The oldest manuscripts for "shall have delivered up," read, "delivereth up," which suits the sense better. It is "when He shall have put down all rule," that "He delivereth up the kingdom to the Father."<div eID="gen33893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall have put down all rule--</hi>the effect produced during the millennary reign of Himself and His saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6">8:6</reference>; 2:6-9), to which passages Paul refers, resting his argument on the two words, "all" and "until," of the Psalmist: a proof of verbal inspiration of Scripture (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26">Re 2:26</reference>, 27). Meanwhile, He "rules in the midst of His enemies" (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>). He is styled "the King" when He takes His great power (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">Mt 25:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.17">17</reference>). The Greek for "put down" is, "done away with," or "brought to naught." "All" must be subject to Him, whether openly opposed powers, as Satan and his angels, or kings and angelic principalities (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>). <div eID="gen33894" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc800d65cdbd8cf50fbde12c5b889beb605aeb9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17112"/><div sID="gen33895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17112"/><hi type="bold">25. must--</hi>because Scripture foretells it.<div eID="gen33895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till--</hi>There will be no further need of His mediatorial kingdom, its object having been realized.<div eID="gen33896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enemies under his feet--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.19.27">Lu 19:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Ep 1:22</reference>). <div eID="gen33897" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8bfe7e63ee8780b2224ddfb53240933e6e19c4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17113"/><div sID="gen33898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17113"/><hi type="bold">26. shall be--</hi>Greek, "is done away with" (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.14">Re 20:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Re 1:18</reference>). It is to believers especially this applies (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55-1Cor.15.57">1Co 15:55-57</reference>); even in the case of unbelievers, death is done away with by the general resurrection. Satan brought in sin, and sin brought in death! So they shall be destroyed (rendered utterly powerless) in the same order (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.56">1Co 15:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">Re 19:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.10">20:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen33898" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ffd4753e224b09793ea149d97fc4125d2cfc0d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17114"/><div sID="gen33899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17114"/><hi type="bold">27. all things--</hi>including death (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Ep 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.8">He 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>). It is said, "hath put," for what God has said is the same as if it were already done, so sure is it. Paul here quotes <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6">Psa 8:6</reference> in proof of his previous declaration, "For (it is written), 'He hath put all things under His feet.'"<div eID="gen33899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under his feet--</hi>as His footstool (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>). In perfect and lasting subjection.<div eID="gen33900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he--</hi>namely, God, who by His Spirit inspired the Psalmist. <div eID="gen33901" type="x-p"/>
entries.52b9355424a5b7594d01b9b23476406d06067ce4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17115"/><div sID="gen33902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17115"/><hi type="bold">28. Son ... himself ... subject--</hi>not as the creatures are, but as a Son voluntarily subordinate to, though co-equal with, the Father. In the mediatorial kingdom, the Son had been, in a manner, distinct from the Father. Now, His kingdom shall merge in the Father's, with whom He is one; not that there is thus any derogation from His honor; for the Father Himself wills "that all should honor the Son, as they honor the Father" (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">He 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen33902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God ... all in all--</hi>as Christ is all in all (<reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col 3:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>). Then, and not till then, "all things," without the least infringement of the divine prerogative, shall be subject to the Son, and the Son subordinate to the Father, while co-equally sharing His glory. Contrast <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">14:1</reference>. Even the saints do not fully realize God as their "all" (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.25">Psa 73:25</reference>) now, through desiring it; then each shall feel, God is all to me. <div eID="gen33903" type="x-p"/>
entries.295b129a272a5ddd60fb2e4d2a7445df22908f90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17116"/><div sID="gen33904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17116"/><hi type="bold">29. Else--</hi>if there be no resurrection.<div eID="gen33904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what shall they do?--</hi>How wretched is their lot!<div eID="gen33905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... which are baptized for the dead--</hi>third person; a class distinct from that in which the apostle places himself, "we" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.30">1Co 15:30</reference>); first person. Alford thinks there is an allusion to a practice at Corinth of baptizing a living person in behalf of a friend who died unbaptized; thus Paul, without giving the least sanction to the practice, uses an ad hominem argument from it against its practicers, some of whom, though using it, denied the resurrection: "What account can they give of their practice; why are they at the trouble of it, if the dead rise not?" [So Jesus used an ad hominem argument, Mt 12:27]. But if so, it is strange there is no direct censure of it. Some Marcionites adopted the practice at a later period, probably from taking this passage, as Alford does; but, generally, it was unknown in the Church. Bengel translates, "over (immediately upon) the dead," that is, who will be gathered to the dead immediately after baptism. Compare <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference>, "the graves are ready for me." The price they get for their trouble is, that they should be gathered to the dead for ever (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.13">1Co 15:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.16">16</reference>). Many in the ancient Church put off baptism till near death. This seems the better view; though there may have been some rites of symbolical baptism at Corinth, now unknown, perhaps grounded on Jesus' words (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.22">Mt 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.23">23</reference>), which Paul here alludes to. The best punctuation is, "If the dead rise not at all, why are they then baptized for them" (so the oldest manuscripts read the last words, instead of "for the dead")? <div eID="gen33906" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba0c61a3e957f056ffb30c34a8ccb70a04178dd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17117"/><div sID="gen33907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17117"/><hi type="bold">30. we--</hi>apostles (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.9">1Co 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>). A gradation from those who could only for a little time enjoy this life (that is, those baptized at the point of death), to us, who could enjoy it longer, if we had not renounced the world for Christ [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33907" type="x-p"/>
entries.22f38cbaa24c2d4f4ae41f891ed6c51925adf278: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17118"/><div sID="gen33908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17118"/><hi type="bold">31. by your rejoicing--</hi>by the glorying which I have concerning you, as the fruit of my labors in the Lord. Some of the earliest manuscripts and fathers read "our," with the same sense. Bengel understands "your rejoicing," to be the enjoyable state of the Corinthians, as contrasted with his dying daily to give his converts rejoicing or glorying (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">1Co 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">2Co 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">Ep 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.26">Php 1:26</reference>). But the words, "which I have," favor the explanation--"the rejoicing which I have over you." Many of the oldest manuscripts and Vulgate insert "brethren" here.<div eID="gen33908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I die daily--</hi>This ought to stand first in the sentence, as it is so put prominently forward in the Greek. I am day by day in sight of death, exposed to it, and expecting it (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">1:8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">11:23</reference>). <div eID="gen33909" type="x-p"/>
entries.26b3db0ab238199cd1c7a49c777f700d19dc46f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17119"/><div sID="gen33910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17119"/>32. Punctuate thus: "If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantageth it me? If the dead rise not, let us eat and drink," &c. [Bengel]. If "merely as a man" (with the mere human hope of the present life; not with the Christian's hope of the resurrection; answering to "If the dead rise not," the parallel clause in the next sentence), I have fought with men resembling savage beasts. Heraclitus, of Ephesus, had termed his countrymen "wild beasts" four hundred years before. So Epimenides called the Cretians (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>). Paul was still at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.8">1Co 16:8</reference>), and there his life was daily in danger (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">2Co 1:8</reference>). Though the tumult (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.30">30</reference>) had not yet taken place (for after it he set out immediately for Macedonia), this Epistle was written evidently just before it, when the storm was gathering; "many adversaries" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">1Co 16:9</reference>) were already menacing him.<div eID="gen33910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what advantageth it me?--</hi>seeing I have renounced all that, "as a mere man," might compensate me for such sufferings, gain, fame, &c.<div eID="gen33911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let us eat, &c.--</hi>Quoted from the Septuagint, (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Is 22:13</reference>), where the prophet describes the reckless self-indulgence of the despisers of God's call to mourning, Let us enjoy the good things of life now, for it soon will end. Paul imitates the language of such skeptics, to reprove both their theory and practice. "If men but persuade themselves that they shall die like the beasts, they soon will live like beasts too" [South]. <div eID="gen33912" type="x-p"/>
entries.19031b3399b9ba06268b762f139b2b4b3cc6c6a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17120"/><div sID="gen33913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17120"/><hi type="bold">33. evil communications corrupt good manners--</hi>a current saying, forming a verse in Menander, the comic poet, who probably took it from Euripides [Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, 3.16]. "Evil communications" refer to intercourse with those who deny the resurrection. Their notion seems to have been that the resurrection is merely spiritual, that sin has its seat solely in the body, and will be left behind when the soul leaves it, if, indeed, the soul survive death at all.<div eID="gen33913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good--</hi>not only good-natured, but pliant. Intimacy with the profligate society around was apt to corrupt the principles of the Corinthians. <div eID="gen33914" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1eb4a9f034fbf106a8867b08d92b9342137d92c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17121"/><div sID="gen33915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17121"/><hi type="bold">34. Awake--</hi>literally, "out of the sleep" of carnal intoxication into which ye are thrown by the influence of these skeptics (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.5">Joe 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen33915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to righteousness--</hi>in contrast with "sin" in this verse, and corrupt manners (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>).<div eID="gen33916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin not--</hi>Do not give yourselves up to sinful pleasures. The Greek expresses a continued state of abstinence from sin. Thus, Paul implies that they who live in sinful pleasures readily persuade themselves of what they wish, namely, that there is to be no resurrection.<div eID="gen33917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">some--</hi>the same as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.12">1Co 15:12</reference>.<div eID="gen33918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have not the knowledge of God--</hi>and so know not His power in the resurrection (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.29">Mt 22:29</reference>). Stronger than "are ignorant of God." An habitual ignorance: wilful, in that they prefer to keep their sins, rather than part with them, in order to know God (compare <reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.15">1Pe 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to your shame--</hi>that you Corinthian Christians, who boast of your knowledge, should have among you, and maintain intercourse with, those so practically ignorant of God, as to deny the resurrection. <div eID="gen33920" type="x-p"/>
entries.457f7446a81582fc30ae12c3630e751704e23ffc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17122"/><div sID="gen33921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17122"/><hi type="bold">35. How--</hi>It is folly to deny a fact of REVELATION, because we do not know the "how." Some measure God's power by their petty intelligence, and won't admit, even on His assurance, anything which they cannot explain. Ezekiel's answer of faith to the question is the truly wise one (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.3">Eze 37:3</reference>). So Jesus argues not on principles of philosophy, but wholly from "the power of God," as declared by the Word of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.26">Mt 19:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.27">Mr 10:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.12.23">12:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.27">Lu 18:27</reference>).<div eID="gen33921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come--</hi>The dead are said to depart, or to be deceased: those rising again to come. The objector could not understand how the dead are to rise, and with what kind of a body they are to come. Is it to be the same body? If so, how is this, since the resurrection bodies will not eat or drink, or beget children, as the natural bodies do? Besides, the latter have mouldered into dust. How then can they rise again? If it be a different body, how can the personal identity be preserved? Paul answers, In one sense it will be the same body, in another, a distinct body. It will be a body, but a spiritual, not a natural, body. <div eID="gen33922" type="x-p"/>
entries.c25b05861472c09ad839bbc32fb703d059710c46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17123"/><div sID="gen33923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17123"/><hi type="bold">36. fool--</hi>with all thy boasted philosophy (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>).<div eID="gen33923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which thou--</hi>"thou," emphatical: appeal to the objector's own experience: "The seed which thou thyself sowest." Paul, in this verse and in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.42">1Co 15:42</reference>, answers the question of <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.35">1Co 15:35</reference>, "How?" and in 1Co 15:37-41, 43, the question, "With what kind of body?" He converts the very objection (the death of the natural body) into an argument. Death, so far from preventing quickening, is the necessary prelude and prognostication of it, just as the seed "is not quickened" into a new sprout with increased produce, "except it die" (except a dissolution of its previous organization takes place). Christ by His death for us has not given us a reprieve from death as to the life which we have from Adam; nay, He permits the law to take its course on our fleshly nature; but He brings from Himself new spiritual and heavenly life out of death (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.37">1Co 15:37</reference>). <div eID="gen33924" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d1e55846beb791b9a74ed031cf111bdcc749c04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17124"/><div sID="gen33925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17124"/><hi type="bold">37. not that body that shall be--</hi>a body beautiful and no longer a "bare grain" [Bengel]. No longer without stalk or ear, but clothed with blade and ears, and yielding many grains instead of only one [Grotius]. There is not an identity of all the particles of the old and the new body. For the perpetual transmutation of matter is inconsistent with this. But there is a hidden germ which constitutes the identity of body amidst all outward changes: the outward accretions fall off in its development, while the germ remains the same. Every such germ ("seed," <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.38">1Co 15:38</reference>) "shall have its own body," and be instantly recognized, just as each plant now is known from the seed that was sown (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1Co 6:13</reference>). So Christ by the same image illustrated the truth that His death was the necessary prelude of His putting on His glorified body, which is the ground of the regeneration of the many who believe (<reference osisRef="John.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference>). Progress is the law of the spiritual, as of the natural world. Death is the avenue not to mere revivification or reanimation, but to resurrection and regeneration (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>). Compare "planted," &c., <reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>. <div eID="gen33925" type="x-p"/>
entries.298ea507d214b4fd146f29a35bb9611acd8dc26b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17125"/><div sID="gen33926" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17125"/><hi type="bold">38. as it hath pleased him--</hi>at creation, when He gave to each of the (kinds of) seeds (so the Greek is for "to every seed") a body of its own (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.11">Ge 1:11</reference>, "after its kind," suited to its species). So God can and will give to the blessed at the resurrection their own appropriate body, such as it pleases Him, and such as is suitable to their glorified state: a body peculiar to the individual, substantially the same as the body sown. <div eID="gen33926" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cb0d861e60cfdebceb9f90f1294e147d2ff8d5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17126"/><div sID="gen33927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17126"/>39-41. Illustrations of the suitability of bodies, however various, to their species: the flesh of the several species of animals; bodies celestial and terrestrial; the various kinds of light in the sun, moon, and stars, respectively.<div eID="gen33927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>animal organism [De Wette]. He implies by the word that our resurrection bodies shall be in some sense really flesh, not mere phantoms of air [Estius]. So some of the oldest creeds expressed it, "I believe in the resurrection of the flesh." Compare as to Jesus' own resurrection body, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.39">Lu 24:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.27">Joh 20:27</reference>; to which ours shall be made like, and therefore shall be flesh, but not of animal organism (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>) and liable to corruption. But <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.50">1Co 15:50</reference> below implies, it is not "flesh and blood" in the animal sense we now understand them; for these "shall not inherit the kingdom of God."<div eID="gen33928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not the same--</hi>not flesh of the same nature and excellency. As the kinds of flesh, however widely differing from one another, do not cease to be flesh, so the kinds of bodies, however differing from one another, are still bodies. All this is to illustrate the difference of the new celestial body from its terrestrial seed, while retaining a substantial identity.<div eID="gen33929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beasts--</hi>quadrupeds.<div eID="gen33930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">another of fishes ... another of birds--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts read thus, "another FLESH of birds ... another of fishes": the order of nature. <div eID="gen33931" type="x-p"/>
entries.8eccc13bed27f87db71b2dfc33ea77ae5f46df53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17129"/><div sID="gen33936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17129"/><hi type="bold">42. sown--</hi>Following up the image of seed. A delightful word instead of burial.<div eID="gen33936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in corruption--</hi>liable to corruption: corruptible: not merely a prey when dead to corruption; as the contrast shows, "raised in incorruption," that is, not liable to corruption: incorruptible. <div eID="gen33937" type="x-p"/>
entries.23077395b84c740de5776303a4512c94a5dfbc6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17130"/><div sID="gen33938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17130"/><hi type="bold">43. in dishonour--</hi>answering to "our vile body" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>); literally, "our body of humiliation": liable to various humiliations of disease, injury, and decay at last.<div eID="gen33938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in glory--</hi>the garment of incorruption (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.42">1Co 15:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.43">43</reference>) like His glorious body (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.21">Php 4:21</reference>), which we shall put on (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.49">1Co 15:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.53">53</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2-2Cor.5.4">2Co 5:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen33939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in weakness--</hi>liable to infirmities (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.4">2Co 13:4</reference>).<div eID="gen33940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in power--</hi>answering to a "spiritual body" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44">1Co 15:44</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Lu 1:17</reference>, "Spirit and power"). Not liable to the weaknesses of our present frail bodies (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Is 33:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Re 21:4</reference>). <div eID="gen33941" type="x-p"/>
entries.f25a52153d48bdcab7c7c5057a1c090e3aae2678: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17131"/><div sID="gen33942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17131"/><hi type="bold">44. a natural body--</hi>literally, "an animal body," a body moulded in its organism of "flesh and blood" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.50">1Co 15:50</reference>) to suit the animal soul which predominates in it. The Holy Spirit in the spirit of believers, indeed, is an earnest of a superior state (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>), but meanwhile in the body the animal soul preponderates; hereafter the Spirit shall predominate, and the animal soul be duly subordinate.<div eID="gen33942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spiritual body--</hi>a body wholly moulded by the Spirit, and its organism not conformed to the lower and animal (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.35">Lu 20:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">36</reference>), but to the higher and spiritual, life (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>).<div eID="gen33943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">There is, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "IF there is a natural (or animal-souled) body, there is also a spiritual body." It is no more wonderful a thing, that there should be a body fitted to the capacities and want of man's highest part, his spirit (which we see to be the case), than that there should be one fitted to the capacities and wants of his subordinate part, the animal soul [Alford]. <div eID="gen33944" type="x-p"/>
entries.179eab5eaaf82272c1e5bd105cfee3c382b8646b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17132"/><div sID="gen33945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17132"/><hi type="bold">45. so--</hi>in accordance with the distinction just mentioned between the natural or animal-souled body and the spiritual body.<div eID="gen33945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is written--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Ge 2:7</reference>); "Man became (was made to become) a living soul," that is, endowed with an animal soul, the living principle of his body.<div eID="gen33946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the last Adam--</hi>the LAST Head of humanity, who is to be fully manifested in the last day, which is His day (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">Joh 6:39</reference>). He is so called in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.14">Ro 5:14</reference>). In contrast to "the last," Paul calls "man" (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Ge 2:7</reference>) "the FIRST Adam."<div eID="gen33947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quickening--</hi>not only living, but making alive (<reference osisRef="John.5.21">Joh 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.33">6:33</reference>, 39, 40, 54, 57, 62, 63; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>). As the natural or animal-souled body (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44">1Co 15:44</reference>) is the fruit of our union with the first Adam, an animal-souled man, so the spiritual body is the fruit of our union with the second Adam, who is the quickening Spirit (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2Co 3:17</reference>). As He became representative of the whole of humanity in His union of the two natures, He exhausted in His own person the sentence of death passed on all men, and giveth spiritual and everlasting life to whom He will. <div eID="gen33948" type="x-p"/>
entries.deb28ab1629949be2ad1c3f973a7dfa5706c9306: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17133"/><div sID="gen33949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17133"/><hi type="bold">46. afterward--</hi>Adam had a soul not necessarily mortal, as it afterwards became by sin, but "a living soul," and destined to live for ever, if he had eaten of the tree of life (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.22">Ge 3:22</reference>); still his body was but an animal-souled body, not a spiritual body, such as believers shall have; much less was he a "life-giving spirit," as Christ. His soul had the germ of the Spirit, rather than the fulness of it, such as man shall have when restored "body, soul, and spirit," by the second Adam (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>). As the first and lower Adam came before the second and heavenly Adam, so the animal-souled body comes first, and must die before it be changed into the spiritual body (that is, that in which the Spirit predominates over the animal soul). <div eID="gen33949" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6d49009ac46cb78dd6e65783aee4d12628bb947: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17134"/><div sID="gen33950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17134"/><hi type="bold">47. of the earth--</hi>inasmuch as being sprung from the earth, he is "earthy" (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Ge 2:7</reference>; 3:19, "dust thou art"); that is, not merely earthly or born upon the earth, but terrene, or of earth; literally, "of heaped earth" or clay. "Adam" means red earth.<div eID="gen33950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts and versions.<div eID="gen33951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from heaven--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.31">31</reference>). Humanity in Christ is generic. In Him man is impersonated in his true ideal as God originally designed him. Christ is the representative man, the federal head of redeemed man. <div eID="gen33952" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7425a0f5bdbbede3ab5199c771cdff241f2a348: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17135"/><div sID="gen33953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17135"/><hi type="bold">48. As is the earthy--</hi>namely, Adam.<div eID="gen33953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... that are earthy--</hi>All Adam's posterity in their natural state (<reference osisRef="John.3.6">Joh 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen33954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the heavenly--</hi>Christ.<div eID="gen33955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... that are heavenly--</hi>His people in their regenerate state (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">21</reference>). As the former precedes the latter state, so the natural bodies precede the spiritual bodies. <div eID="gen33956" type="x-p"/>
entries.df018a26f541351bad45092190f1b526e3a38740: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17136"/><div sID="gen33957" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17136"/><hi type="bold">49. as--</hi>Greek, "even as" (see <reference osisRef="Gen.5.3">Ge 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen33957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we shall also bear--</hi>or wear as a garment [Bengel]. The oldest manuscripts and versions read, "We must also bear," or "let us also bear." It implies the divine appointment (compare "must," <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.53">1Co 15:53</reference>) and faith assenting to it. An exhortation, and yet implying a promise (so <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>). The conformity to the image of the heavenly Representative man is to be begun here in our souls, in part, and shall be perfected at the resurrection in both bodies and souls. <div eID="gen33958" type="x-p"/>
entries.f53fd0a4bd1ef3c018315937b56fae135f72f219: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17137"/><div sID="gen33959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17137"/>50. (See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.37">1Co 15:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.39">1Co 15:39</reference>). "Flesh and blood" of the same animal and corruptible nature as our present (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44">1Co 15:44</reference>) animal-souled bodies, cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Therefore the believer acquiesces gladly in the unrepealed sentence of the holy law, which appoints the death of the present body as the necessary preliminary to the resurrection body of glory. Hence he "dies daily" to the flesh and to the world, as the necessary condition to his regeneration here and hereafter (<reference osisRef="John.3.6">Joh 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>). As the being born of the flesh constitutes a child of Adam, so the being born of the Spirit constitutes a child of God.<div eID="gen33959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot--</hi>Not merely is the change of body possible, but it is necessary. The spirit extracted from the dregs of wine does not so much differ from them, as the glorified man does from the mortal man [Bengel] of mere animal flesh and blood (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.16">Ga 1:16</reference>). The resurrection body will be still a body though spiritual, and substantially retaining the personal identity; as is proved by <reference osisRef="Luke.24.39">Lu 24:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.27">Joh 20:27</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>.<div eID="gen33960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the kingdom of God--</hi>which is not at all merely animal, but altogether spiritual. Corruption doth not inherit, though it is the way to, incorruption (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.36">1Co 15:36</reference>, 52, 53). <div eID="gen33961" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ceeae703ed9533586d9eef009a325788b40a448: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17138"/><div sID="gen33962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17138"/><hi type="bold">51. Behold--</hi>Calling attention to the "mystery" heretofore hidden in God's purposes, but now revealed.<div eID="gen33962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you--</hi>emphatical in the Greek; I show (Greek, "tell," namely, by the word of the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">1Th 4:15</reference>) YOU, who think you have so much knowledge, "a mystery" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference>) which your reason could never have discovered. Many of the old manuscripts and Fathers read, "We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed"; but this is plainly a corrupt reading, inconsistent with <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">1Th 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">17</reference>, and with the apostle's argument here, which is that a change is necessary (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.53">1Co 15:53</reference>). English Version is supported by some of the oldest manuscripts and Fathers. The Greek is literally "We all shall not sleep, but," &c. The putting off of the corruptible body for an incorruptible by an instantaneous change will, in the case of "the quick," stand as equivalent to death, appointed to all men (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.27">He 9:27</reference>); of this Enoch and Elijah are types and forerunners. The "we" implies that Christians in that age and every successive age since and hereafter were designed to stand waiting, as if Christ might come again in their time, and as if they might be found among "the quick." <div eID="gen33963" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7794ead3bbddaa4a94588d58d7007a014979018: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17139"/><div sID="gen33964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17139"/><hi type="bold">52. the last trump--</hi>at the sounding of the trumpet on the last day [Vatablus] (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">Mt 24:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>). Or the Spirit by Paul hints that the other trumpets mentioned subsequently in the Apocalypse shall precede, and that this shall be the last of all (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Is 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.14">Zec 9:14</reference>). As the law was given with the sound of a trumpet, so the final judgment according to it (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.19">He 12:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Ex 19:16</reference>). As the Lord ascended "with the sound of a trumpet" (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference>), so He shall descend (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>). The trumpet was sounded to convoke the people on solemn feasts, especially on the first day of the seventh month (the type of the completion of time; seven being the number for perfection; on the tenth of the same month was the atonement, and on the fifteenth the feast of tabernacles, commemorative of completed salvation out of the spiritual Egypt, compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18">Zec 14:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.19">19</reference>); compare <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1-Ps.50.7">Psa 50:1-7</reference>. Compare His calling forth of Lazarus from the grave "with a loud voice," <reference osisRef="John.11.43">Joh 11:43</reference>, with <reference osisRef="John.5.25">Joh 5:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.28">28</reference>.<div eID="gen33964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>immediately, in consequence. <div eID="gen33965" type="x-p"/>
entries.63b8f53ecad48197cab644585c1c918559a6b3a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17140"/><div sID="gen33966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17140"/><hi type="bold">53. this--</hi>pointing to his own body and that of those whom he addresses.<div eID="gen33966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put on--</hi>as a garment (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">2Co 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen33967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">immortality--</hi>Here only, besides <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>, the word "immortality" is found. Nowhere is the immortality of the soul, distinct from the body, taught; a notion which many erroneously have derived from heathen philosophers. Scripture does not contemplate the anomalous state brought about by death, as the consummation to be earnestly looked for (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">2Co 5:4</reference>), but the resurrection. <div eID="gen33968" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cf806ae16846d55ef56ae273e9198878aaa31b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17141"/><div sID="gen33969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17141"/><hi type="bold">54. then--</hi>not before. Death has as yet a sting even to the believer, in that his body is to be under its power till the resurrection. But then the sting and power of death shall cease for ever.<div eID="gen33969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Death is swallowed up in victory--</hi>In Hebrew of <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Is 25:8</reference>, from which it is quoted, "He (Jehovah) will swallow up death in victory"; that is, for ever: as "in victory" often means in Hebrew idiom (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jr 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.20">La 5:20</reference>).
