The apostle insinuates, that it was by a mixture of the corrupt communications of these men with the Christian Church, and the intimate contact into which they had permitted themselves to come with them, that they had been led off from the fundamental doctrine of the gospel, and rejected a primary part of the apostolic testimony. ‘For if there be no resurrection of the dead, then,’ as he observed, ‘is Christ not risen, and if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain; ye are yet in your sins.’ We see, that notwithstanding the apostle had planted pure Christianity among the Corinthians, and had confirmed it by the most extraordinary miracles and supernatural operations, yet such was the contagion of evil example and corrupt communication, that the members of the Corinthian Church, in a very short time, departed from the fundamental article of the truth as it is in Jesus Christ; and hence we may learn the importance, nay, the necessity, of being on our guard in this respect, and of avoiding such confidence in ourselves as might induce us to neglect the caution here so forcibly expressed — ’Be not deceived; evil communications corrupt good manners.’” — <hi type="italic">R. Hall’s Works, </hi>(Lond. 1846,) volume 6, pages 273, 274. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120296" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120293" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120288" osisID="1Cor.15.33" type="section"/>
entries.9eebf34fb0473c13057970ee4fc28ea156330d20:
34. Awake righteously As he saw that the Corinthians were in a manner intoxicated,
The original word ἐκνήψατε, properly signifies to awake sober out of a drunken sleepage It is used in this sense in stone instances in the Septuagint. Thus in Joel 1:5, Εκνηψατε οἱ μεθυντες Awake, ye drunkards. See also Genesis 9:24, and 1 Samuel 25:37. It is used in the same sense by classical writers. “‘Awake to righteousness and sin not, for some have not the knowledge of God. I speak this to your shame;’ that is, shake off the mental delusion and stupor in which the intoxication of error has involved you, that, with clear and exerted faculties, you may attend to the most important subject.” — Brown’s Expository Discourses on Peter, volume in. page 8. The expression ἐκνήψατε δικαίως, (awake righteously,) is rendered by Luther machet recht aui — “Wake right up.” It is, however, generally considered to be elliptical. Some supply ζησοτες — “Awake, that ye may live righteously. Others understand δικαίως, as equivalent to ὡς δικαίως δεῖ “as it is fit you should.” “Arrian and Menander,” says Parkhurst, “use δικαιως in this sense, as may be seen in Alberti on the text.” To the two authorities quoted by Alberti, Alexander in his Paraphrase on 1 Corinthians xv., adds one from Ocellus Lucanus — ̔Ο δε διαμαχομενος δικαιως, but the man who stands up for his own authority as he ought to do.” — Apud Gale, page 533, I. 20. Ed. 1688. — Ed.
through excessive carelessness, he arouses them from their torpor. By adding, however, the adverb righteously, he intimates in what way he would have them wake up For they were sufficiently attentive and clear-sighted as to their own affairs: nay more, there can be no doubt that they congratulated themselves on their acuteness; but in the mean time they were drowsy, where they ought most of all to have been on the watch. He says accordingly, awake righteously — that is, “Direct your mind and aim to things that are good and holy.”
He adds at the same time the reason, — For some, says he, among you are in ignorance of God This required to be stated: otherwise they might have thought that the admonition was unnecessary; for they looked upon themselves as marvellously wise. Now he convicts them of ignorance of God, that they may know that the main thing was wanting in them. A useful admonition to those who lay out all their agility in flying through the air, while in the mean time they do not see what is before their feet, and are stupid where they ought, most of all, to have been clear-sighted.
To your shame Just as fathers, when reproving their children for their faults, put them to shame, in order that they may by that shame cover their shame. When, however, he declared previously that he did not wish to shame them, (1 Corinthians 4:14,) his meaning was that he did not wish to hold them up to disgrace, by bringing forward their faults to public view in a spirit of enmity and hatred.
See Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 1, p. 167.
In the mean time, however, it was of advantage for them to be sharply reproved, as they were still indulging themselves in evils of such magnitude. Now Paul in reproaching them with ignorance of God, strips them entirely of all honor.
1 Corinthians 15:35-50
35. But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?
35. Sed dicet quispiam: Quomodo suscitabuntur mortui? quali nutem corpore venient?
36. Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die:
36. Demens, tu quod seminas, non vivificatur nisi mortuum fuerit.
37. And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain:
37. Et quod seminas, non corpus quod nascentur, seminas, sed nudum granum: exempli gratis, tritici, nut alterius cujusvis generis:
38. But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.
38. Deus autem illi dat corpus, quemadmodum voluerit, et unicuique seminum proprium corpus.
39. All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
39. Non omnis caro, eadem caro: sed alia caro hominum, alia vero cato pecudum, alia volucrum, alia piscium.
40. There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.
40. Sunt et corpora coelestia, sunt corpora terrestria: quin etiam alia coelestium gloria, alia terrestrium.
41. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.
41. Alia gloria solis, alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarum: stella a stella differt in gloria:
42. So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
42. Sic et resurrectio mortuorum. Seminatur in corruptione, re surgit in incorruptione:
The Latin text "Seminatur in corruptione, re surgit in incorruptione:" in the original manuscript was at the beginning of verse 43, I have moved it to match the Vulgate (possible error in the Edinburgh edition.) — fj.
43. It is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power:
43. Seminatur in ignominia, resurgit in gloria: seminatur in infirmitate, resurgit in potentia:
44. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
44. Seminatur corpus animale, resurgit corpus spirituale: est corpus animale, est et corpus spirituale.
45. And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.
45. Quemadmodum et scriptum eat, (Gen 2:7,) Factus est primus homo Adam in animam viventem, ultimus Adam in spiritum vivificantem.
46. Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual.
46. Sed non primum quod spirituale est: sed animale, deinde spirituale.
47. The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
47. Primus homo ex terra terrenus, secundus homo, Dominus e coelo.
48. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
48. Qualis terrenus, tales et terreni, et qualis coelestis, tales et coelestes.
49. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
49. Et quemadmodum portavimus imaginem terreni, portabimus et imaginem coelestis.
50. Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption.
50. Hoc autem dico, fratres, quod cato et sanguis regnum Dei hereditate possidere non possunt, neque corruptio incorruptionem hereditate possidebit.
entries.d0806bf121c9e0cf63d1d142e0b10d6cf51419ad:
35. How will they be raised up? There is nothing that is more at variance with human reason than this article of faith. For who but God alone could persuade us that bodies, which are now liable to corruption, will, after having rotted away, or after they have been consumed by fire, or torn in pieces by wild beasts, will not merely be restored entire, but in a greatly better condition. Do not all our apprehensions of things straightway reject this as a thing fabulous, nay, most absurd?
“Comme la plus grande absux, dite du monde;” — “As the greatest absurdity in the world.”
Paul, with the view of removing entirely this appearance of absurdity, makes use of an anhypophora,
See Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 1, p. 281, n. 1.
that is, he brings forward by way of objection, in the person of another, what appears at first view to be at variance with the doctrine of a resurrection. For this question is not that of one who inquires doubtingly as to the mode, but of one who argues from impossibility — that is, what is said as to the resurrection is a thing incredible. Hence in his reply he repels such an objection with severity. Let us observe, then, that the persons who are here introduced as speaking, are those who endeavor to disparage, in a way of scoffing, a belief in the resurrection, on the ground of its being a thing that is impossible.
entries.be8de7663e178bb0d568c12392dcccb9e3bd8180: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.36" sID="gen120343" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">36.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thou fool, that which thou sowest</hi> The Apostle might have replied, that the mode, which is to us incomprehensible, is nevertheless easy with God. Hence, we must not here form our judgment according to our own understanding, but must assign to the stupendous and secret power of God the honor of believing, that it will accomplish what we cannot comprehend. He goes to work, however, in another way. For he shows, that the resurrection is so far from being against nature, that we have every day a clear illustration of it in the course of nature itself — in the growth of the fruits of the earth. For from what but from rottenness spring the fruits that we gather out of the earth? For when the seed has been sown, unless the grains <hi type="italic">die, </hi>there will be no increase. Corruption, then, being the commencement and cause of production, we have in this a sort of picture of the resurrection. Hence it follows, that we are beyond measure spiteful and ungrateful in estimating the power of God, if we take from him what is already manifest before our eyes.<div eID="gen120344" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120343" osisID="1Cor.15.36" type="section"/>
entries.a6cb7e8284e8d8647e49b6c2da1f4fbc1c626555: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.37" sID="gen120345" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thou sowest not that body that will spring up.</hi> This comparison consists of two <hi type="italic">parts</hi> — <hi type="italic">first, </hi>that it is not to be wondered that bodies rise from rottenness, inasmuch as the same thing takes place as to seed; and <hi type="italic">secondly, </hi>that it is not at variance with reason, that our bodies should be restored in another condition, since, from bare grain, God brings forth so many ears of corn, clothed with admirable contrivance, and stored with grains of superior quality. As, however, he might seem to intimate, by speaking in this way, that many bodies will therefore rise out of one, he modifies his discourse in another way, by saying that God <hi type="italic">forms the body as it pleases him, </hi>meaning that in that also there is a difference in respect of quality.<div eID="gen120346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120347" type="x-p"/>He adds, <hi type="italic">to every seed its own body</hi> By this clause he restricts what he had said respecting another body; for he says that, while the body is different, it is in such a way as to retain, nevertheless, its particular kind.<div eID="gen120347" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120345" osisID="1Cor.15.37" type="section"/>
entries.d31994aceb96b367f55d9673fb8c86ee66ffd57f: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.39" sID="gen120348" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">39.</hi> <hi type="italic">All flesh is not, etc</hi>. Here we have another comparison leading to the same conclusion, though there are some that explain it otherwise. For when he says, that under the name of<hi type="italic"> flesh </hi>is comprehended the body of a man as well as of a beast, and yet the <hi type="italic">flesh </hi>in those two cases is different, he means by this that the substance indeed is the same, but there is a difference as to quality. The sum is this — that whatever diversity we see in any particular kind is a sort of prelude of the resurrection, because God clearly shows, that it is no difficult thing with him to renew our bodies by changing the present condition of things. <note n="102"> <div sID="gen120350" type="x-p"/> “Nearly allied to these are the examples of peculiar transformations undergone by various insects, and the state of rest and insensibility which precede those transformations; such as the chrysalis or aurelia state of butterflies, moths, and silkworms. The <foreign xml:lang="la">myrmeleon forniicaleo</foreign>, of whose larva, and its extraordinary history, Reaumur and Roesel have given accurate descriptions, continues in its insensible or chrysalis state about four weeks. The <foreign xml:lang="la">libellula</foreign>, or dragon-fly, continues still longer in its state of inaction. Naturalists tell us that the worm repairs to the margin of its pond, in quest of a convenient place of abode, during its insensible state. It attaches itself to a plant, or piece of dry wood, and the skin, which gradually becomes parched and brittle, at last splits opposite to the upper part of the thorax: through this aperture the insect, now become winged, quickly pushes its way, and being thus extricated front confinement, begins to expand its wings, to flutter, and, finally, to launch into the air with that gracefulness and ease which are peculiar to this majestic tribe. Now who that saw, for the first time, the little pendant coffin in which the insect lay entombed, and was ignorant of the transformation of which we are now speaking, would ever predict that, in a few weeks, perhaps in a few days or hours, it would become one of the most elegant and active of <hi type="italic">winged </hi>insects? And who that contemplates, with the mind of a philosopher, this current transformation, and knows that two years before the insect mounts into the air, even while it is living in water, it has the rudiments of wings, can deny that the body of a dead man may, at some future period, be again invested with vigor and activity, and soar to regions for which some latent organization may have peculiarly fitted it?” — <hi type="italic">Olythus Gregory’s </hi>Letters on the Evidences of the Christian Religion, page 225. — Ed.<div eID="gen120350" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120349" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120348" osisID="1Cor.15.39" type="section"/>
entries.b38dd0af70761d0d388a714326a202205f88fd4d: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.41" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.41" sID="gen120351" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">41.</hi> <hi type="italic">There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon</hi> Not only is there a difference between heavenly bodies and earthly, but even the heavenly bodies have not all the same glory; for the sun surpasses the moon, and the other stars differ from each other. This dissimilarity, accordingly, appears <note n="103"> <div sID="gen120353" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ceste dinersite de qualite se monstre</foreign>;” — “This difference of quality shows itself.”<div eID="gen120353" type="x-p"/> </note> in the <hi type="italic">resurrection </hi>of the dead. A mistake, however, is commonly fallen into in the application; <note n="104"> <div sID="gen120354" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En l’application de ceste similitude</foreign>;” — “In the application of this similitude.”<div eID="gen120354" type="x-p"/> </note> for it is supposed that Paul meant to say, that, after the resurrection, the saints will have different degrees of honor and glory. This, indeed, is perfectly true, and is proved by other declarations of Scripture; but it has nothing to do with Paul’s object. For he is not arguing as to what difference of condition there will be among the saints after the resurrection, but in what respect our bodies at present differ from those that we will one day receive. <note n="105"> <div sID="gen120355" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comment different nos corps que nons auons maintenant de ceux que nons aurons apres</foreign>;” — “In what respect our bodies, which we have now, will differ from those that we shall have afterwards.”<div eID="gen120355" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120356" type="x-p"/>He removes, then, every idea of absurdity, by instituting this comparison: The substance of the sun and moon is the same, but there is a great difference between them in point of dignity and excellence. Is it to be wondered, then, if our body puts on a more excellent quality? <note n="106"> <div sID="gen120357" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qu’il n’ha maintenant</foreign>;” — “Than it has now.”<div eID="gen120357" type="x-p"/> </note> “I do not teach that anything will take place at the resurrection but what is already presented before the eyes of all.” That such is the meaning of the words is clear from the context. For whence and for what purpose would Paul make such a transition, were he now comparing them with one another in respect of the difference of their condition, while up to this point he has been comparing the present condition of all with their future condition, and immediately proceeds with that comparison?<div eID="gen120356" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.41" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120351" osisID="1Cor.15.41" type="section"/>
entries.9086d217e340878065883d01302eb30369cf2605: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.43" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.43" sID="gen120358" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">43.</hi> <hi type="italic">It is sown in corruption</hi> That there may be no doubt remaining, Paul explains himself, by unfolding the difference between their present condition, and that which will be after the resurrection. What connection, then, would there be in his discourse, if he had intended in the first instance <note n="107"> <div sID="gen120360" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Au propos precedent</foreign>;” — “In the foregoing statement.”<div eID="gen120360" type="x-p"/> </note> to distinguish between the different degrees of future glory among the saints? There can, therefore, be no doubt, that he has been, up to this point, following out one subject. He now returns to the first similitude that he had made use of, but applies it more closely to his design. Or, if you prefer it, keeping up that similitude, he figuratively compares the time of the present life to the seed-time, and the resurrection to the harvest; and he says, that our body is now, indeed, subject to mortality and ignominy, but will then be glorious and incorruptible. He says the same thing in other words in <reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.21">Philippians 3:21</reference><div eID="gen120359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120361" type="x-p"/>Christ will change our vile body,<lb/> that he may make it like to his own glorious body.<div eID="gen120361" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.43" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120358" osisID="1Cor.15.43" type="section"/>
entries.9ff8241aef50356945e208014829f259c89e89da: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.44" sID="gen120362" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">44. </hi><hi type="italic">It is sown an animal body.</hi> As he could not express <hi type="italic">each </hi>particular by enumerating one by one, he sums up all <hi type="italic">comprehensively </hi>in one word, by saying that the body is now <hi type="italic">animal,</hi> <note n="108"> <div sID="gen120364" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">It </hi>is generally agreed on by the best expositors, that <foreign xml:lang="el">ψυχικὸς</foreign> here, as being opposed to <foreign xml:lang="el">πευματικὸς</foreign><hi type="italic">, (spiritual,) </hi>especially as the expression is used with a reference to the words of Moses respecting the body of Adam, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐγένετο εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν </foreign><hi type="italic">(became a living soul,) </hi>must signify <hi type="italic">animal, </hi>(literally that which draws in the breath of life, necessary to the existence of all animal bodies,) that which is endowed with faculties of sense, and has need of food, drink, and sleep for its <hi type="italic">support.”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Bloomfield.</hi> “<foreign xml:lang="el">Ψυχικὸν </foreign>not <foreign xml:lang="el">φυσικὸν</foreign>. (says <hi type="italic">Granville Penn,) </hi>and therefore not ‘<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">naturale</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">’ </hi>but ‘<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">animale</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">,’ </hi>as rendered in the Latin. Wiclif,” (he adds,) <hi type="italic">“strangely </hi>rendered, from the Vulg., ‘<hi type="italic">a beastli bodi,</hi>’ in correcting whom, our revisers would have done well to prefer ‘<hi type="italic">animal’ </hi>to ‘<hi type="italic">natural.’”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120364" type="x-p"/> </note> but it will then be <hi type="italic">spiritual. </hi>Now that is called <hi type="italic">animal </hi>which is quickened by <hi type="italic">(</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">anima</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">) </hi>the soul: that is <hi type="italic">spiritual </hi>which is quickened by the <hi type="italic">Spirit.</hi> <note n="109"> <div sID="gen120365" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Au reste la ou nous traduisons, Sensuel, il y auroit a le tourner au plus pres du Grec, Animal: c’est a dire, gouuerne et viuifie de l’ame. Voyla donc que signifie Le corps sensuel. Le corps spirituel est celuy qui est viuifie de l’Esprit</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>But what we translate <hi type="italic">sensual, </hi>might be rendered, more closely to the Greek, <hi type="italic">animal: </hi>that is to say, governed and quickened by the soul. Mark then what is meant by <hi type="italic">the sensual body. </hi>The spiritual body is that which is quickened by the Spirit.”<div eID="gen120365" type="x-p"/> </note> Now it is the soul that quickens the body, so as to keep it from being a dead carcase. Hence it takes its title very properly from it. After the resurrection, on the other hand, that quickening influence, which it will receive from the Spirit, will be more excellent. <note n="110"> <div sID="gen120366" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sera vne chose beaucoup plus excellente</foreign>;” — “Will be a thing much more excellent.”<div eID="gen120366" type="x-p"/> </note> Let us, however, always bear in mind, what we have seen previously — that the substance of the body is the same, <note n="111"> <div sID="gen120367" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La substance du corps sera tousiours vne</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>The substance of the body will always be the same.”<div eID="gen120367" type="x-p"/> </note> and that it is the quality only that is here treated of. Let the present quality of the body be called, for the sake of greater plainness, <hi type="italic">animation;</hi> <note n="112"> <div sID="gen120368" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Animation</hi>, qui est nom descendant de ce mot <hi type="italic">Ame</hi></foreign>;” — “<hi type="italic">Animation, </hi>which is a name derived from this word <hi type="italic">Soul</hi>.”<div eID="gen120368" type="x-p"/> </note> let the future receive the name of <hi type="italic">inspiration. </hi>For as to the soul’s now <hi type="italic">quickening </hi>the body, that is effected through the intervention of many helps; for we stand in need of drink, food, clothing, sleep, and other things of a similar nature. Hence the weakness of <hi type="italic">animation </hi>is clearly manifested. The energy of the Spirit, on the other hand, for <hi type="italic">quickening, </hi>will be much more complete, and, consequently, exempted from necessities of that nature. This is the simple and genuine meaning of the Apostle; that no one may, by philosophizing farther, indulge in airy speculations, as those do, who suppose that the substance of the body will be spiritual, while there is no mention made here of substance, and no change will be made upon it.<div eID="gen120363" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120362" osisID="1Cor.15.44" type="section"/>
entries.d941dfd8955f3fca3047427f1c49e3e71650ea08: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.45" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.45" sID="gen120369" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">45.</hi> <hi type="italic">As it is written, The first Adam was made</hi> Lest it should seem to be some new contrivance as to the <hi type="italic">animal body,</hi> <note n="113"> <div sID="gen120371" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne nouuelle imagination qu’il ait forgee</foreign>;” — “A new fancy that he had contrived.”<div eID="gen120371" type="x-p"/> </note> he quotes Scripture, which declares that Adam <hi type="italic">became a living soul, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.7">Genesis 2:7</reference>) — meaning, that his body was quickened by the soul, so that he became a living man. It is asked, what is the meaning of the word <hi type="italic">soul </hi>here? It is well known, that the Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">נפש</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(nephesh,) </hi>which Moses makes use of, is taken in a variety of senses; but in this passage it is taken to mean either vital motion, or the <hi type="italic">very</hi> <hi type="italic">essence </hi>of life itself. The second of these I rather prefer. I observe that the same thing is affirmed as to beasts — that they were made <hi type="italic">a living soul, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.20 Bible:Gen.1.24">Genesis 1:20, 24</reference>;) but as the soul of every animal must be judged of according to its kind, there is nothing to hinder that a <hi type="italic">soul, </hi>that is to say, vital motion, may be common to all; and yet at the same time the <hi type="italic">soul </hi>of man may have something peculiar and distinguishing, namely, immortal <hi type="italic">essence, </hi>as the light of intelligence and reason.<div eID="gen120370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120372" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The last Adam.</hi> This expression we do not find anywhere <hi type="italic">written.</hi> <note n="114"> <div sID="gen120373" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ceci n’est point trouue en lieu quelconque de l’Escriture</foreign>;” — “This is not found in any passage of Scripture.”<div eID="gen120373" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence the phrase,<hi type="italic"> It is written, </hi>must be understood as referring exclusively to the first clause; but after bringing forward this testimony of Scripture, the Apostle now begins in his own person to draw a contrast between Christ and Adam. <hi type="italic">“Moses </hi>relates that Adam was furnished with a <hi type="italic">living soul; </hi>Christ, on the other hand, is endowed with a <hi type="italic">life-giving Spirit. </hi>Now it is a much greater thing to be <hi type="italic">life, </hi>or the <hi type="italic">source of life, </hi>than simply to <hi type="italic">live.”</hi> <note n="115"> <div sID="gen120374" type="x-p"/> “As it is said, Adam was at first <hi type="italic">a living soul, </hi>(‘So God breathed into him the breath of life,’ — that pure, divine, and heavenly breath,) ‘and he became a living soul;’ so, then to have asked the question, ‘What is man?’ must have been to receive the answer, ‘He is a <hi type="italic">living soul: </hi>he is all soul, and that soul all life.’ But now is this living soul buried in flesh, a lost thing to all the true, and great, and noble ends and purposes of that life which was at first given it. It is true, indeed, that this is a thing much less than what is said of the second Adam, in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.45">1 Corinthians 15:45</reference>. ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul; the second Adam was a quickening Spirit.’ This latter is a great deal more. A <hi type="italic">living soul </hi>signified him to live himself; but a quickening spirit signifies a power to make others live. <hi type="italic">That </hi>the first Adam could not do; the more excellent kind of life which he had (for there was a complication of lives in the first creation of this man) he could not <hi type="italic">lose: </hi>but he could not <hi type="italic">give. </hi>He could not <hi type="italic">lose </hi>it from himself; but he could never have <hi type="italic">given </hi>it, by any power or immediate efficiency of his own, to another. Here the second Adam — the constitution of the second Adam — was far above that of the first, in that he could quicken others — a <hi type="italic">quickening spirit, </hi>not only quickened passively, but quickened actively, such a spirit as could give spirit, and diffuse life.” — Howe’s Works, (Lond. 1834,) page 1209. — Ed.<div eID="gen120374" type="x-p"/> </note> It must be observed, however, that Christ did also, like us, become a <hi type="italic">living soul; </hi>but, besides the <hi type="italic">soul, </hi>the Spirit of the Lord was also poured-out upon him, that by his power he might rise again from the dead, and raise up others, This, therefore, must be observed, in order that no one may imagine, (as Apollinaris <note n="116"> <div sID="gen120375" type="x-p"/> The views held by Apollinaris were as follows: “<foreign xml:lang="la">Christum corpus assumpsisse sine anima, quod pro anima ei fuerit deitas illudque corpus consubstantiale fuisse deitati, nec ex substantia Martin efformatum</foreign>;” — “That Christ assumed a body without a stud, because Deity was to him in place of a stud, and that body was co-essential with Deity, and was not formed from the substance of Mary.” — See Mastrieht’s Theology, (1698,) volume ii. page 975. “Apollinaris, or Apollinarius, taught that the Son of God assumed manhood <hi type="italic">without a soul, (</hi><foreign xml:lang="el">ψυχης ανευ</foreign>,) as Socrates relates; but afterwards, changing his mind, he said that he assumed a soul, but that it <hi type="italic">did not possess the intelligent or rational principle, </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">νουν δε ουκ εξεις αυτην</foreign>) and that the <foreign xml:lang="el">λογος</foreign> <hi type="italic">(word) </hi>was <hi type="italic">instead of that principle, (</hi><foreign xml:lang="el">αντιςου</foreign><hi type="italic">)”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Dick’s </hi>Lectures on Theology volume iii. page <hi type="italic">22.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120375" type="x-p"/> </note> did of old,) that the Spirit was in Christ in place of a soul. And independently of this, the interpretation of this passage may be taken from the eighth chapter of the Romans, where the Apostle declares, that <hi type="italic">the body, indeed, is dead, on account of sin, </hi>and we <hi type="italic">carry</hi> in us the elements of death; but that <hi type="italic">the Spirit of Christ, who raised him up from the dead, dwelleth also in us, </hi>and that he is life, to raise up us also one day from the dead. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.10 Bible:Rom.8.11">Romans 8:10, 11</reference>.) From this you see, that we have <hi type="italic">living souls, </hi>inasmuch as we are men, but that we have the <hi type="italic">life-giving Spirit </hi>of Christ poured out upon us by the grace of regeneration. In short, Paul’s meaning is, that the condition that we obtain through Christ is greatly superior to the lot of the <hi type="italic">first man, </hi>because a <hi type="italic">living soul </hi>was conferred upon Adam in his own name, and in that of his posterity, but Christ has procured for us the Spirit, who is <hi type="italic">life.</hi><div eID="gen120372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120376" type="x-p"/>Now as to his calling Christ <hi type="italic">the last Adam, </hi>the reason is this, that as the human race was created in the <hi type="italic">first man, </hi>so it is renewed in Christ. I shall express it again, and more distinctly: All men were created in the <hi type="italic">first man, </hi>because, whatever God designed to give to all, he conferred upon that one man, so that the condition of mankind was settled in his person. He by his fall <note n="117"> <div sID="gen120377" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le poure mal-heureux par sa transgression</foreign>;” — “The poor miserable creature by his transgression.”<div eID="gen120377" type="x-p"/> </note> ruined himself and those that were his, because he drew them all, along with himself, into the same ruin: Christ came to restore our nature from ruin, and raise it up to a better condition than ever. They <note n="118"> <div sID="gen120378" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Adam done et Christ</foreign>;” — “Adam and Christ, therefore.”<div eID="gen120378" type="x-p"/> </note> are then, as it were, two sources, or two roots of the human race. Hence it is not without good reason, that the one is called the <hi type="italic">first man, </hi>and the other the <hi type="italic">last. </hi>This, however, gives no support to those madmen, who make Christ to be one of ourselves, as though there were and always had been only two men, and that this multitude which we behold, were a mere phantom! A similar comparison occurs in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.12">Romans 5:12</reference><div eID="gen120376" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.45" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120369" osisID="1Cor.15.45" type="section"/>
entries.b43a539f93c54c74e13e42c92d42d4a1258b0bbe: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.46" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.46" sID="gen120379" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">46.</hi> <hi type="italic">But this is not first, which is spiritual.</hi> “It is necessary,” says he, “that before we are restored in Christ, we derive our origin from Adam, and resemble him. Let us, therefore, not wonder, if we begin with the <hi type="italic">living soul, </hi>for as <hi type="italic">being born</hi> precedes in order <hi type="italic">being born again, </hi>so <hi type="italic">living </hi>precedes <hi type="italic">rising again.”</hi><div eID="gen120380" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.46" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120379" osisID="1Cor.15.46" type="section"/>
entries.626af245b31c970398c536fbc56211f4b37236c1: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.47" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.47" sID="gen120381" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">47.</hi> <hi type="italic">The first Adam was from the earth.</hi> The <hi type="italic">animal </hi>life comes first, because the <hi type="italic">earthy man </hi>is first. <note n="119"> <div sID="gen120383" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La vie sensuelle, ou animale, c’est a dire, que nous auons par le moyen de l’ame, precede</foreign>;” — “The sensual or animal life, that is to say, what we have by means of the soul, comes first.”<div eID="gen120383" type="x-p"/> </note> The spiritual life will come afterwards, as Christ, the <hi type="italic">heavenly man, </hi>came after Adam. Now the Manichees perverted this passage, with the view of proving that Christ brought a body from heaven into the womb of the Virgin. They mistakingly imagined, however, that Paul speaks here of the substance of the body, while he is discoursing rather as to its condition, or quality. Hence, although the <hi type="italic">first man </hi>had an immortal soul, and that too, not taken from the earth, yet he, nevertheless, savoured of the earth, from which his body had sprung, and on which he had been appointed to live. Christ, on the other hand, brought us from heaven a <hi type="italic">life-giving Spirit, </hi>that he might regenerate us into a better life, and elevated above the earth. <note n="120"> <div sID="gen120384" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Plus haute et excellente que la terre</foreign>;” — “Higher and more excellent than the earth.”<div eID="gen120384" type="x-p"/> </note> In fine, we have it from Adam — that we live in this world, as branches from the root: Christ, on the other hand, is the beginning and author of the heavenly life.<div eID="gen120382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120385" type="x-p"/>But some one will say in reply, Adam is said to be <hi type="italic">from the earth</hi> — Christ<hi type="italic"> from heaven; </hi>the nature of the comparison <note n="121"> <div sID="gen120386" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La nature de l’antithese et comparison</foreign>;” — “The nature of the contrast and comparison.”<div eID="gen120386" type="x-p"/> </note> requires this much, that Christ have his body <hi type="italic">from heaven, </hi>as the body of Adam was formed <hi type="italic">from the earth; </hi>or, at least, that the origin of man’s soul should be <hi type="italic">from the earth, </hi>but that Christ’s soul had come forth from heaven. I answer, that Paul had not contrasted the two departments of the subject with such refinement and minuteness, (for this was not necessary;) but when treating of the nature of Christ and <hi type="italic">Adam, </hi>he made a passing allusion to the creation of Adam, that he had been formed <hi type="italic">from the earth,, </hi>and at the same time, for the purpose of commending Christ’s excellence, he states, that he is the Son of God, who came down to us from heaven, and brings with him, therefore, a heavenly nature and influence. This is the simple meaning, while the refinement of the Manichees is a mere calumny.<div eID="gen120385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120387" type="x-p"/>We must, however, reply to another objection still. For Christ, so long as he lived in the world, lived a life similar to ours, and therefore earthly: hence it is not a proper contrast. The solution of this question will serve farther to refute the contrivance <note n="122"> <div sID="gen120388" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La meschante imagination</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>The wicked fancy.”<div eID="gen120388" type="x-p"/> </note> of the Manichees. For we know, that the body of Christ was liable to death, and that it was exempted from corruption, not by its essential property, (as they speak,) <note n="123"> <div sID="gen120389" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Afin que Fuse du terme commun</foreign>;” — “To use the common phrase.”<div eID="gen120389" type="x-p"/> </note> but solely by the providence of God. Hence Christ was not merely <hi type="italic">earthy </hi>as to the essence of his body, but was also for a time in an earthly condition; for before Christ’s power could show itself in conferring the heavenly life, it was necessary that he should die in the <hi type="italic">weakness of the flesh, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.13.4">2 Corinthians 13:4</reference>.) Now this heavenly life appeared first in the resurrection, that he might quicken us also.<div eID="gen120387" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.47" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120381" osisID="1Cor.15.47" type="section"/>
entries.ace48b4cfc92094cf15c98d8e296265b04c932af: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.49" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.49" sID="gen120390" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">49.</hi> <hi type="italic">As we have borne</hi> Some have thought, that there is here an exhortation to a pious and holy life, into which Paul was led by way of digression; and on that account they have changed the verb from the future tense into the hortative mood. Nay more, in some Greek manuscripts the reading is <foreign xml:lang="el">φορέσωμεν</foreign> <hi type="italic">(let us bear,)</hi> <note n="124"> <div sID="gen120392" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pourtant en lieu de <hi type="italic">Nous porterons, </hi>aucuns ont traduit <hi type="italic">Portons. </hi>Et mesme aucuns liures Grecs le lisent ainsi</foreign>;” — “Hence instead of <hi type="italic">We shall bear, </hi>some have rendered it, <hi type="italic">Let us bear. </hi>And even some Greek manuscripts read it thus.”<div eID="gen120392" type="x-p"/> </note> but as that does not suit so well in respect of connection, let us adopt in preference what corresponds better with the object in view and the context. <note n="125"> <div sID="gen120393" type="x-p"/> The Alexandrine manuscript, with some others, reads <foreign xml:lang="el">φορέσωμεν</foreign>, <hi type="italic">let us bear. </hi>The rendering of the Vulgate is <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">portemus</hi></foreign> — <hi type="italic">(let us bear.) </hi>Wiclif (1380) following the Vulgate, as he is wont, renders as follows: <hi type="italic">bere we also the ymage of the heuenli.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120393" type="x-p"/> </note> Let us observe, in the first place, that this is not an exhortation, but pure doctrine, and that he is not treating here of newness of life, but pursues, without any interruption, the thread of his discourse respecting the resurrection of the flesh. The meaning accordingly will be this: “As the <hi type="italic">animal nature, </hi>which has the <hi type="italic">precedency </hi>in us, is the image of Adam, so we shall be conformed to Christ in the <hi type="italic">heavenly nature; </hi>and this will be the completion of our restoration. For we <hi type="italic">now </hi>begin to bear the image of Christ, and are every day more and more transformed into it; <note n="126"> <div sID="gen120394" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car nons ne faisons encore que commencer a porter l’image de Jesus Christ</foreign>;” — “For as yet we do but begin to bear the image of Jesus Christ.”<div eID="gen120394" type="x-p"/> </note> but that image consists in spiritual regeneration. But <hi type="italic">then </hi>it will be fully restored both in body and in soul, and what is now begun will be perfected, and <hi type="italic">accordingly </hi>we will obtain in reality what we as yet only hope for.” If, however, any one prefers a different reading, this statement will serve to spur forward the Corinthians; and if there had been a lively meditation of sincere piety and a new life, it might have been the means of kindling up in them at the same time the hope of heavenly glory.<div eID="gen120391" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.49" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120390" osisID="1Cor.15.49" type="section"/>
entries.f248a8f5b9821a30d0c28d0604a8893cc97653af:
50. Now this I say This clause intimates, that what follows is explanatory of the foregoing statement. “What I have said as to bearing the image of the heavenly Adam means this — that we must be renewed in respect of our bodies, inasmuch as our bodies, being liable to corruption, cannot inherit God’s incorruptible kingdom. Hence there will be no admission for us into the kingdom of Christ, otherwise than by Christ’s renewing us after his own image.” Flesh and blood, however, we must understand, according to the condition in which they at present are, for our flesh will be a participant in the glory of God, but it will be — as renewed and quickened by the Spirit of Christ.
1 Corinthians 15:51-58
51. Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
51. Ecce, mysterium vobis dico: Non omnes quidem dormiemus, omnes tamen immutabimur,
52. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
52. In puncto temporis, in nictu oculi, cum extrema tuba, (canet enim tuba,) et mortui resurgent incorruptibiles, et nos immutabimur.
53. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
53. Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere immortalitatem.
54. So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.
54. Quum autem corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, et mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem: tunc flet sermo qui scriptus est: (Hosea 13, 14, vel les. 25, 8.) Absorpta est mors in victoriam.
55. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
55. Ubi, mors, tuus aculeus? Ubi tua, inferne, victoria?
56. The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law.
56. Aculeus autem mortis, peccatum est: virtus autem peccati, Lex.
57. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
57. Sed Deo gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
58. Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
58. Itaque, fratres mei dilecti, stabiles sitis, immobiles, abundantes in opere Domini semper, hoc cognifo, quod labor vester non sit inanis in Domino.
entries.290a9dc81952ae7c13349b3e1e79d77e13060b54: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.51" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.51" sID="gen120416" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120417" type="x-p"/>Hitherto he has included two things in his reasoning. In <hi type="italic">the first </hi>place, he shows that there will be a resurrection from the dead: <hi type="italic">secondly, </hi>he shows of what nature it will be. Now, however, he enters more thoroughly into a description of the manner of it. This he calls a <hi type="italic">mystery, </hi>because it had not been as yet so clearly unfolded in any statement of revelation; but he does this to make them more attentive. For that wicked doctrine had derived strength from the circumstance, that they disputed as to this matter carelessly and at their ease; <note n="127"> <div sID="gen120418" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par maniere de passe-temps, et tout a leur aise</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>By way of pastime, and quite at their ease.”<div eID="gen120418" type="x-p"/> </note> as if it were a matter in which they felt no difficulty. Hence by the term <hi type="italic">mystery, </hi>he admonishes them to learn a matter, which was not only as yet unknown to them, but ought to be reckoned among God’s heavenly secrets.<div eID="gen120417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">51. </hi><hi type="italic">We shall not indeed all sleep.</hi> Here there is no difference in the Greek manuscripts, but in the Latin versions there are three different readings. The <hi type="italic">first </hi>is, <hi type="italic">We shall indeed all die, but we shall not all be changed. </hi>The <hi type="italic">second </hi>is, <hi type="italic">We shall indeed all rise again, but we shall not all be changed.</hi> <note n="128"> <div sID="gen120420" type="x-p"/> This is the reading of the Vulgate. Wiclif (1380) translates the verse as follows: Lo, I seie to you pryuyte (secret) of holi things, and alle we schulen rise agen, but not alle we schulen be chaungid. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120420" type="x-p"/> </note> The <hi type="italic">third </hi>is, <hi type="italic">We shall not indeed all sleep, but we shall all be changed. </hi>This diversity, I conjecture, had arisen from this — that some readers, who were not the most discerning, dissatisfied with the true reading, ventured to conjecture a reading which was more approved by them. <note n="129"> <div sID="gen120421" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui leur estoit plus probable</foreign>;” — “Which appeared to them more probable.”<div eID="gen120421" type="x-p"/> </note> For it appeared to them, at first view, to be absurd to say, that <hi type="italic">all would not die, </hi>while we read elsewhere, that <hi type="italic">it is appointed unto all men once to die. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.27">Hebrews 9:27</reference>.) Hence they altered the meaning in this way — All <hi type="italic">will not be changed, though all will rise again, or will die; </hi>and the <hi type="italic">change </hi>they interpret to mean — the glory that the sons of God alone will obtain. The true reading, however, may be judged of from the context.<div eID="gen120419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120422" type="x-p"/>Paul’s intention is to explain what he had said — that we will be conformed to Christ, because <hi type="italic">flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.</hi> A question presented itself, <note n="130"> <div sID="gen120423" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il y auoit sur ceci vne question qu’on prouuolt faire</foreign>;” — “There was a question as to this, which might be proposed.”<div eID="gen120423" type="x-p"/> </note> what then will become of those who will be still living at the day of the Lord? His answer is, that although <hi type="italic">all will not die, </hi>yet they will be renewed, that mortality and corruption may be done <hi type="italic">away. </hi>It is to be observed, however, that he speaks exclusively of believers; for although the resurrection of the wicked will also involve <hi type="italic">change, </hi>yet as there is no mention made of them here, we must consider everything that is said, as referring exclusively to the elect. We now see, how well this statement corresponds with the preceding one, for as he had said, that <hi type="italic">we shall bear the image of Christ, </hi>he now declares, that this will take place when we shall be <hi type="italic">changed, </hi>so that<div eID="gen120422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120424" type="x-p"/>mortality may be swallowed up of life, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.4">2 Corinthians 5:4</reference>,)<div eID="gen120424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120425" type="x-p"/>and that this renovation is not inconsistent with the fact, that Christ’s advent will find some still alive.<div eID="gen120425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120426" type="x-p"/>We must, however, unravel the difficulty — that <hi type="italic">it is appointed unto all men once to die; </hi>and certainly, it is not difficult to unravel it in this way — that as a <hi type="italic">change </hi>cannot take place without doing away with the previous system, that <hi type="italic">change </hi>is reckoned, with good reason, a kind of <hi type="italic">death; </hi>but, as it is not a separation of the soul from the body, it is not looked upon as an ordinary death. It will then be <hi type="italic">death, </hi>inasmuch as it will be the destruction of corruptible nature: it will not be a <hi type="italic">sleep, </hi>inasmuch as the soul will not quit the body; but there will be a sudden transition from corruptible nature into a blessed immortality.<div eID="gen120426" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.51" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120416" osisID="1Cor.15.51" type="section"/>
entries.873ef1a4b442df291b4284683835f927be0dc496: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.52" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.52" sID="gen120427" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">52. </hi><hi type="italic">In a moment</hi> This is still of a general nature; that is, it includes all. For in all the change will be sudden and instantaneous, because Christ’s advent will be sudden. And to convey the idea of <hi type="italic">a moment, </hi>he afterwards makes use of the phrase <hi type="italic">twinkling </hi>(or <hi type="italic">jerk) </hi>of the eye, for in the Greek manuscripts there is a twofold, reading — <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥοπὣ</foreign> <hi type="italic">(jerk,) </hi>or <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥιπὣ</foreign> <hi type="italic">(twinkling.)</hi> <note n="131"> <div sID="gen120429" type="x-p"/> It is stated by <hi type="italic">Semlr, </hi>that some in the times of Jerome preferred <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥοπὟ</foreign>, but Jerome himself preferred <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥιπὟ</foreign> is derived from <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥέπω</foreign>, to tend or incline to. It means <hi type="italic">force </hi>or <hi type="italic">impetus. </hi>It is used by Thucydides (v. 103) to mean the preponderance of <hi type="italic">a scale. </hi>In connection with <foreign xml:lang="el">ὀφθαλμοῦ</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(the eye,) </hi>it would probably mean, a <hi type="italic">cast </hi>or <hi type="italic">inclination </hi>of the eye. <foreign xml:lang="el">̔ΡιπὟ</foreign>, (the common reading,) is derived from <foreign xml:lang="el">ῥίπτω</foreign>, to <hi type="italic">throw. </hi><foreign xml:lang="el">̔ριπὟ ὀφθαλμοῦ </foreign>is explained by <hi type="italic">Nyssenus, </hi>(as stated by <hi type="italic">Parkhurst,) </hi>to mean — <foreign xml:lang="el">επιμύσις</foreign>—<hi type="italic"> the shutting or twinkling of the eyelids.</hi><div eID="gen120429" type="x-p"/> </note> It matters nothing, however, as to the sense. Paul has selected a movement of the body, that surpasses all others in quickness; for nothing is more rapid than a movement of the eye, though at the same time he has made an allusion to <hi type="italic">sleep, </hi>with which <hi type="italic">twinkling of the eye</hi> is contrasted. <note n="132"> <div sID="gen120430" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour ce que quand on se resueille, on cleigne ainsi des yeux</foreign>;” — “Because, when persons awake, they twinkle in this way with their eyes.”<div eID="gen120430" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120431" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">With the last trump.</hi> Though the repetition of the term might seem to place it beyond a doubt, that the word <hi type="italic">trumpet</hi> is here taken in its proper acceptation, yet I prefer to understand the expression as metaphorical. In <reference osisRef="Bible:1Thess.4.16">1 Thessalonians 4:16</reference>, he connects together the <hi type="italic">voice of the archangel </hi>and the <hi type="italic">trump of God: </hi>As therefore a commander, with the sound of a trumpet, summons his army to battle, so Christ, by his far sounding proclamation, which will be heard throughout the whole world, will summon all the dead. Moses tells us, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.16">Exodus 19:16</reference>,) what loud and terrible sounds were uttered on occasion of the promulgation of the law. Far different will be the commotion <hi type="italic">then, </hi>when not one people merely, but the whole world will be summoned to the tribunal of God. Nor will the living only be convoked, but even the dead will be called forth from their graves. <note n="133"> <div sID="gen120432" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The trumpet shall sound, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.52">1 Corinthians 15:52</reference>,) says the prophetic teacher. And how startling, how stupendous the summons! Nothing equal to it, nothing like it, was ever heard through all the regions of the universe, or all the revolutions of time. When conflicting armies have discharged the bellowing artillery of war, or when victorious armies have shouted for joy of the conquest, the seas and shores have rung, the mountains and plains have echoed. But the shout of the archangel, and the trump of God, will resound from pole to poles — will pierce the center and shake the pillars of heaven. Stronger — stronger still — it will penetrate even the deepest recesses of the tomb! It will pour its amazing thunder into all those abodes of silence. The dead, the very dead, shall <hi type="italic">hear.”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Hervey’s </hi>Theron and Aspasio, volume 2 page <hi type="italic">66.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120432" type="x-p"/> </note> Nay more, a commandment must be given to dry bones and dust that, resuming their former appearance and reunited to the spirit, they come forth straightway as living men into the presence of Christ.<div eID="gen120431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120433" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The dead shall rise</hi> What he had declared generally as to all, he now explains particularly as to the living and the dead. This distinction, therefore, is simply an exposition of the foregoing statement — <hi type="italic">that all will not die, but all will be changed</hi> “Those who have already died,” says he, <hi type="italic">“will </hi>rise again incorruptible.” See what a change there will be upon the <hi type="italic">dead! </hi>“Those,” says he, “who will be still alive will themselves also be <hi type="italic">changed.” </hi>You see then as to both. <note n="134"> <div sID="gen120434" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Voyla donc ques les viuans et les morts</foreign>;” — “Mark then how it will be as to the living and the dead.”<div eID="gen120434" type="x-p"/> </note> You now then perceive how it is, that <hi type="italic">change </hi>will be common to all, but not <hi type="italic">sleep.</hi> <note n="135"> <div sID="gen120435" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Non pus le dormir, c’est a dire la mort</foreign>;” — “Not sleep, that is to say, death.”<div eID="gen120435" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120436" type="x-p"/>When he says, <hi type="italic">We shall be changed, </hi>he includes himself in the number of those, who are to live till the advent of Christ. As it was now the <hi type="italic">last times, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.2.18">1 John 2:18</reference>,) <hi type="italic">that day </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:2Tim.1.18">2 Timothy 1:18</reference>) was to be looked for by the saints every hour. At the same time, in writing to the Thessalonians, he utters that memorable prediction respecting the scattering <note n="136"> <div sID="gen120437" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La dissipation horrible</foreign>;” — “The dreadful scattering.”<div eID="gen120437" type="x-p"/> </note> that would take place in the Church before Christ’s coming. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Thess.2.3">2 Thessalonians 2:3</reference>.) This, however, does not hinder that he might, by bringing the Corinthians, as it were, into immediate contact with the event, associate himself and them with those who would at that time be alive.<div eID="gen120436" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.52" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120427" osisID="1Cor.15.52" type="section"/>
entries.9461685f8ce4a30af26af272055bec1621c170bf: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.53" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.53" sID="gen120438" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">53. </hi><hi type="italic">For this corruptible must</hi> Mark, how we shall live in the kingdom of God both in body and in soul, while at the same time <hi type="italic">flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God</hi> — for they shall previously be delivered from corruption. Our nature then, as being now corruptible and mortal, is not admissible into the kingdom of God, but when it shall have put off corruption, and shall have been beautified with in-corruption, it will then make its way into it. This passage, too, distinctly proves, that we shall rise again in that same flesh that we now carry about with us, as the Apostle assigns a new quality to it which will serve as a garment. If he had said, <hi type="italic">This corruptible must be renewed, </hi>the error of those fanatics, who imagine that mankind will be furnished with new bodies, would not have been so plainly or forcibly overthrown. Now, however, when he declares that <hi type="italic">this corruptible shall be invested with glory, </hi>there is no room left for cavil.<div eID="gen120439" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.53" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120438" osisID="1Cor.15.53" type="section"/>
entries.68c7033057c601be41b689d516c182128f9d9f07: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.54" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.54" sID="gen120440" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">54. </hi><hi type="italic">Then shall be brought to pass the saying</hi> This is not merely an amplification, <hi type="italic">(</hi><foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπεξεργασία</foreign><hi type="italic">,)</hi> <note n="137"> <div sID="gen120442" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne declaration ou amplification</foreign>;” — “A declaration or amplification.”<div eID="gen120442" type="x-p"/> </note> but a confirmation, too, of the preceding statement. For what was foretold by the Prophets must be fulfilled. Now this prediction will not be fulfilled, until our bodies, laying aside corruption, will <hi type="italic">put on incorruption</hi> Hence this last result, also, is necessary. To <hi type="italic">come to pass, </hi>is used here in the sense of being <hi type="italic">fully accomplished, </hi>for what Paul quotes is now begun in us, and is daily, too, receiving further accomplishment; but it will not have its complete fulfillment until the last day.<div eID="gen120441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120443" type="x-p"/>It does not, however, appear quite manifest, from what passage he has taken this quotation, for many statements occur in the Prophets to this effect. Only the probability is, that the first clause is taken either from <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.25.8">Isaiah 25:8</reference>, where it is said that <hi type="italic">death will be for ever destroyed </hi>by the Lord, <note n="138"> <div sID="gen120444" type="x-p"/> “The words, as alleged by Paul,” (from <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.25.8">Isaiah 25:8</reference>,) “are found in the version of Theodotion, with which the Targum and Syriac agree, in reading the verb as a passive, <foreign xml:lang="he">כלע</foreign> in Piel, as here, commonly signifies to destroy, <hi type="italic">destroy utterly; </hi>in Kal, the more usual signification is that of <hi type="italic">swallowing, </hi>which most of the versions have unhappily adopted, <foreign xml:lang="he">לנצח</foreign> the Greek translators render by; <foreign xml:lang="el">ἰσχύσας, εἰς τέλος, εἰς νῖκος</foreign>; attaching to the term the idea of what is <hi type="italic">overpowering, durable, complete. </hi>The significations of the Hebrew root <foreign xml:lang="he">נצח</foreign>, used only in Niphal and Piel, are — to <hi type="italic">shine, lead, lead on, be complete; </hi>in Chald. to <hi type="italic">surpass; excel, vanquish; </hi>hence the idea of <hi type="italic">victory, eternity, etc.</hi>, attaching to <foreign xml:lang="he">נצח</foreign>, and of <hi type="italic">completely, entirely, for ever, </hi>etc., to <foreign xml:lang="he">לנצח נצח</foreign>. The words are therefore equivalent <hi type="italic">to </hi><foreign xml:lang="el">ὁ θάνατος ὀυκ ἐσται ἐτι</foreign> — <hi type="italic">(Death shall be no longer,) </hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.4">Revelation 21:4</reference>, where there seems to be an evident allusion to our text; and where the subject is, as here, not the millennial state of the Church, but the state of glory after the resurrection of the body. It will be then only, that a period shall be put to the reproachful persecutions of the righteous, which Isaiah likewise <hi type="italic">predicts.”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Henderson </hi>on Isaiah. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120444" type="x-p"/> </note> or, (as almost all are rather inclined to think,) from <reference osisRef="Bible:Hos.13.14">Hosea 13:14</reference>, where the Prophet, bewailing the obstinate wickedness of Israel, complains that he was like an untimely child, that struggles against the efforts of his mother in travail, that he may not <hi type="italic">come </hi>forth from the womb, and from this he concludes, that it was owing entirely to himself, that he was not delivered from death. <hi type="italic">I will ransom them, </hi>says he, from <hi type="italic">the power of the grave: I will rescue them from death. </hi>It matters not, whether you read these words in the future of the indicative, or in the subjunctive <note n="139"> <div sID="gen120445" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ie les eusse rachetez — ie les eusse deliurez</foreign>;” — “I could have ransomed them — I could have rescued them.”<div eID="gen120445" type="x-p"/> </note> for in either way the meaning amounts to this — that God was prepared to confer upon them salvation, if they would have allowed the favor to be conferred upon them, and that, therefore, if they perished, it was their own fault.<div eID="gen120443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120446" type="x-p"/>He afterwards adds,<hi type="italic"> I will be thy destruction, O death! thy ruin, O grave!</hi> In these words God intimates, that he accomplishes the salvation of his people <note n="140"> <div sID="gen120447" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Lors vrayement et a bon escient il sauue les fideles</foreign>;” — “He then truly and effectually saves believers.”<div eID="gen120447" type="x-p"/> </note> only when death and the grave are reduced to nothing. For no one will deny, that in that passage there is a description of completed salvation. As, therefore, we do not see such a destruction of death, it follows, that we do not yet enjoy that complete salvation, which God promises to his people, and that, consequently, it is delayed until <hi type="italic">that day. Then, </hi>accordingly, <hi type="italic">will death be swallowed up, </hi>that is, it will be reduced to nothing, <note n="141"> <div sID="gen120448" type="x-p"/> “This victory will not be gradual only, but total and entire. Every thing of mortality, that was hanging about these glorious victors, shall be <hi type="italic">swallowed up </hi>in perfect and endless life. Death is unstung first — disarmed — and then easily overcome. Its sting is said to be sin — the deadliest thing in death. A plain farther proof, by the way, the Apostle intended death also in the moral sense. And the insulting inquiry, ‘where is it?’ implies ‘tis not any where to be found; and signifies a total abolition of it, and, by consequence, must infer that every thing of death besides must, as to them, for ever cease and be no more. Which also the phrase of <hi type="italic">swallowing up </hi>doth with great emphasis <hi type="italic">express.”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Howe’s </hi>Works, (Lond. 1834,) page 1035. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120448" type="x-p"/> </note> that we may have manifestly, in every particular, and in every respect, (as they say,) a complete victory over it. <note n="142"> <div sID="gen120449" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En sorte que nons aurons plene et parfaite victoire a Pencontre d’elle</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>So that we shall have a full and complete victory over it.”<div eID="gen120449" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120446" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.54" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120440" osisID="1Cor.15.54" type="section"/>
entries.931ef1d592d67e286ba9418942ade0e0d798e20f: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.55" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.55" sID="gen120450" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120451" type="x-p"/>As to the second clause, in which he triumphs over death and the grave, it is not certain whether he speaks of himself, or whether he meant there also to quote the words of the Prophet. For where we render it, “I will be thy destruction, O death! — thy ruin, O grave<hi type="italic">!” </hi>the Greeks have translated it, “<hi type="italic">Where, O death, is thy suit?</hi> <note n="143"> <div sID="gen120452" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ou est ton plaid, c’est a dire, le proces que tu intentes contre nons, o mort</foreign>?” — “O death, where is thy suit — that is to say, the process that thou carriest on against us?”<div eID="gen120452" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">where, O grave, thy sting?” </hi>Now although this mistake of the Greeks is excusable from the near resemblance of the words, <note n="144"> <div sID="gen120453" type="x-p"/> “The passage (says Dr. Bloomfield) is from <reference osisRef="Bible:Hos.13.14">Hosea 13:14</reference>, and the Apostle’s words differ only by the transposition of <foreign xml:lang="el">νῖκος</foreign> <hi type="italic">(victory) </hi>and <foreign xml:lang="el">κέντρον</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(sting,) </hi>from the ancient versions; except that for <foreign xml:lang="el">νῖκος</foreign> the Sept. has <foreign xml:lang="el">δίκν</foreign> <hi type="italic">(law-suit.)” </hi>It is noticed, however, by <hi type="italic">Granville Penn, </hi>that “in the <hi type="italic">most ancient </hi>of all the existing MSS. (Vat. and <hi type="italic">Ephr.) </hi>there is no <hi type="italic">transposition </hi>of <foreign xml:lang="el">θανατος</foreign> <hi type="italic">(death) </hi>and <foreign xml:lang="el">κεντρον</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(sting;) </hi>and the Apostle’s sentence preserves the same order as in the Greek of Hosea; so that the transposition lies wholly at the door of those MSS. which are <hi type="italic">more recent than those ancient copies.” </hi>The <hi type="italic">Vat. </hi>version has <foreign xml:lang="el">νεικος</foreign>; instead of <foreign xml:lang="el">νικος</foreign>, but from the circumstance that in that version <foreign xml:lang="el">νεικος</foreign> is used in the 54th verse manifestly instead of <foreign xml:lang="el">νικος</foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>it abundantly appears that it is a mere difference of spelling. The words to which Calvin refers, as having been mistaken for each other from their <hi type="italic">near resemblance, </hi>are, <foreign xml:lang="el">δικη</foreign> <hi type="italic">(law-suit) </hi>and <foreign xml:lang="el">νικος</foreign>, (or <foreign xml:lang="el">νικη</foreign>,<hi type="italic">) victory.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120453" type="x-p"/> </note> yet if any one will attentively examine the context, he will see that they have gone quite away from the Prophet’s intention. The true meaning, then, will be this — that the Lord will put an end to death, and destroy the grave. It is possible, however, that, as the Greek translation was in common use, Paul alluded to it, and in that there is nothing inconsistent, though he has not quoted literally, for instead of <hi type="italic">victory </hi>he has used the term <hi type="italic">action, </hi>or <hi type="italic">law-suit.</hi> <note n="145"> <div sID="gen120454" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car en lieu du mot <foreign xml:lang="el">δίκη</foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>qui signifie <hi type="italic">plaid </hi>ou <hi type="italic">proces, </hi>il a mis <foreign xml:lang="el">νῖκος</foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>qui signifie <hi type="italic">victoire</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">;</hi>” — “For in place of the word <foreign xml:lang="el">δίκη</foreign>, which signifies an <hi type="italic">action </hi>or <hi type="italic">law-suit, </hi>they have used <foreign xml:lang="el">νῖκος</foreign>, which signifies <hi type="italic">victory.”</hi><div eID="gen120454" type="x-p"/> </note> I am certainly of opinion, that the Apostle did not deliberately intend to call in the Prophet as a witness, with the view of making a wrong use of his authority, but simply accommodated, in passing, to his own use a sentiment that had come into common use, as being, independently of this, of a pious nature. <note n="146"> <div sID="gen120455" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Bonne et saincte</foreign>;” — “Good and holy,”<div eID="gen120455" type="x-p"/> </note> The main thing is this — that Paul, by an exclamation of a spirited nature, designed to rouse up the minds of the Corinthians, and lead them on, as it were, to a near view of the resurrection. Now, although we do not as yet behold the victory with our eyes, and the day of triumph has not yet arrived, (nay more, the dangers of war must every day be encountered,) yet the assurance of faith, as we shall have occasion to observe ere long, is not at all thereby diminished.<div eID="gen120451" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.55" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120450" osisID="1Cor.15.55" type="section"/>
entries.65de0b8920fea2f84af246ddb48369b9df052e46: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.56" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.56" sID="gen120456" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">56. </hi><hi type="italic">The sting of death is sin</hi> In other words, “Death has no dart with which to wound us except <hi type="italic">sin, </hi>since <hi type="italic">death </hi>proceeds from the anger of God. Now it is only with our sins that God is angry. Take away sin, therefore, and death will no more be able to harm us.” This agrees with what he said in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.23">Romans 6:23</reference>, that <hi type="italic">the wages of sin is death. </hi>Here, however, he makes use of another metaphor, for he compared sin to a <hi type="italic">sting, </hi>with which alone death is armed for inflicting upon us a deadly wound. Let <hi type="italic">that </hi>be taken away, and death is disarmed, so as to be no longer hurtful. Now with what view Paul says this will be explained by him ere long.<div eID="gen120457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120458" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The strength of sin is the law</hi> It is the law of God that imparts to that sting its deadly power, because it does not merely discover our guilt, but even increases it. A clearer exposition of this statement may be found in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.7.9">Romans 7:9</reference>, where Paul teaches us that we <hi type="italic">are alive, </hi>so long as we are <hi type="italic">without the law, </hi>because in our own opinion it is well with us, and we do not feel our own misery, until the law summons us to the judgment of God, and wounds our conscience with an apprehension of eternal death. Farther, he teaches us that sin has been in a manner lulled asleep, but is kindled up by the law, so as to rage furiously. Meanwhile, however, he vindicates the law from calumnies, on the ground that it is <hi type="italic">holy, and good, and just, </hi>and is not of itself the parent of sin or the cause of death. Hence he concludes, that whatever there is of evil is to be reckoned to our own account, inasmuch as it manifestly <hi type="italic">proceeds </hi>from the depravity of our nature. Hence the law is but the <hi type="italic">occasion </hi>of injury. The true <hi type="italic">cause </hi>of ruin is in ourselves. Hence he speaks of the law here as the <hi type="italic">strength or power of sin</hi>, because it executes upon us the judgment of God. In the mean time he does not deny, that sin inflicts death even upon those that know not the law; but he speaks in this manner, because it exercises its tyranny upon them with less violence. For <hi type="italic">the law came that sin might abound, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.20">Romans 5:20</reference>,) or that it <hi type="italic">might become beyond measure sinful. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.7.13">Romans 7:13</reference>.)<div eID="gen120458" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.56" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120456" osisID="1Cor.15.56" type="section"/>
entries.b910613c1dbd501d3bfafdb4f52cb76e5c1042e5: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.57" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.15.57" sID="gen120459" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">57. </hi><hi type="italic">But thanks be to God</hi> From this it appears, why it it was that he made mention both of sin and of the law, when treating of death. Death has no <hi type="italic">sting </hi>with which to wound except <hi type="italic">sin, </hi>and the law imparts to this <hi type="italic">sting </hi>a deadly power. But Christ has conquered sin, and by conquering it has procured victory for us, and <hi type="italic">has</hi> <hi type="italic">redeemed us from the curse of the law. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.13">Galatians 3:13</reference>.) Hence it follows, that we are no longer lying under the power of death. Hence, although we have not as yet a full discovery of those benefits, yet we may already with confidence glory in them, because it is necessary that what has been accomplished in the Head should be accomplished, also, in the members. We may, therefore, triumph over death as subdued, because Christ’s victory is ours.<div eID="gen120460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120461" type="x-p"/>When, therefore, he says, that <hi type="italic">victory has been given to us, </hi>you are to understand by this in the <hi type="italic">first </hi>place, that it is inasmuch as Christ has in his own person abolished sin, has satisfied the law, has endured the curse, has appeased the anger of God, and has procured life; and farther, because he has already begun to make us partakers of all those benefits. For though we still carry about with us the remains of sin, it, nevertheless, does not reign in us: though it still <hi type="italic">stings </hi>us, it does not do so fatally, because its edge is blunted, so that it does not penetrate into the vitals of the soul. Though the law still threatens, yet there is presented to us on the other hand, the liberty that was procured for us by Christ, which is an antidote to its terrors. Though the remains of sin still dwell in us, yet the Spirit who raised up Christ from the dead is <hi type="italic">life, because of righteousness. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.10">Romans 8:10</reference>.) Now follows the conclusion.<div eID="gen120461" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.15.57" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120459" osisID="1Cor.15.57" type="section"/>
